hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10444.context: The text asks where good qualities exist for people who do not have any virtue at all.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10445.meaning: Recognizing good in others is a way to see the Supreme God shining through their actions and spirit.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10445.context: When someone praises all your good qualities, they are actually seeing the divine light in you.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10446.meaning: Wise people avoid the ignorant and use deep study to understand truths that normal minds cannot grasp.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10446.context: The text says true knowledge is beyond normal thinking and is found in deep spiritual study.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10447.meaning: God is beyond our senses and is the eternal, supreme power that exists above all other things.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10447.context: The passage lists many names for God, such as the unmanifest, eternal, and supreme being.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10448.meaning: True skill in spiritual practice comes from understanding the Lord and mastering the twenty five key virtues.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10448.context: The text connects the twenty five virtues and the Lord of deeds to the path of Yoga.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10449.meaning: When you truly understand the hidden truth, you stop fearing life and death and find inner peace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10449.context: Enlightened people understand the hidden state of being and move beyond fear of birth and death.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10450.meaning: True wisdom comes from seeing the whole picture, not just the small, separate parts of life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10450.context: A wise teacher explains that seeing things as separate is a mistake for those seeking truth.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10451.meaning: Everything in the world comes from one source, even though it looks like many different things.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10451.context: The text uses letters as a simple picture to show how one thing can look many ways.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10452.meaning: When your mind is very calm, you stop seeing differences and start seeing the one truth.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10452.context: This verse talks about a special state where all differences disappear and only oneness remains.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10453.meaning: Understanding the basic parts of the world helps you find the deep, unchanging truth inside.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10453.context: Sages discuss the basic building blocks of reality and how they relate to the highest truth.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10454.meaning: It is okay to ask questions when a big idea feels confusing or hard to believe at first.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10454.context: A student asks the teacher for more proof because the idea of one truth is hard to grasp.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10456.meaning: Some deep truths are too big for our normal thinking, so we must stay humble and open.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10456.context: The speaker admits that his ordinary mind cannot fully understand the deep spiritual truths being shared.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10457.meaning: When your mind is busy and restless, it is hard to see the clear light of wisdom.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10457.context: The student feels confused and says the teacher's words seem like darkness because his mind is shaky.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10458.meaning: Learning through practice and discipline can help you understand things that words alone cannot explain.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10458.context: The teacher agrees to explain the practices of yoga to help the king understand these deep ideas.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10517.meaning: All parts of life are linked. Understanding one part helps you understand the whole system.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10517.context: The text explains how different parts of reality are connected and named together.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10518.meaning: When you see the big picture, individual differences fade away. Everything becomes one.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10518.context: The speaker tells his father that all separate parts eventually join into one whole.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10519.meaning: When you see the big picture, individual differences fade away. Everything becomes one.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10519.context: The speaker tells his father that all separate parts eventually join into one whole.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10520.meaning: Your true self is steady. It does not change when outside events happen to you.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10520.context: The text says that true nature stays the same when you stop changing things.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10521.meaning: Knowing the truth sets you free. You are not responsible for what others do.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10521.context: The speaker says he knows the truth about life and is free from blame.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10522.meaning: Real goodness comes from within. You must know who you are to be truly good.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10522.context: The text explains that true goodness comes from knowing your own real nature.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10523.meaning: Stay pure by not copying bad habits. Know that you are separate from others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10523.context: The wise person stays clean by not taking on the faults of other people.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10524.meaning: You are not mixed with others. Your actions are your own, so stay clear and fair.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10524.context: The king is told that he stays separate from the actions of other people.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10572.meaning: True freedom comes from seeing that separate things are really one whole thing.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10572.context: The text explains how two different things can actually be one single truth.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10573.meaning: You become free when you see the hidden truth inside every living body.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10573.context: A person who understands the hidden truth behind all living bodies is free.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10574.meaning: This is the only true path to freedom, and it matches all other faiths.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10574.context: The speaker says this is the only sure way to get free from life.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10575.meaning: Pure duty and truth help your soul join with the higher, free spirit.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10575.context: Wisdom comes from pure duty and pure truth, uniting the soul with the divine.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10577.meaning: Pure actions make your soul shine and help it join with the pure spirit.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10577.context: When actions are pure, the soul shines brightly and joins with the divine.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10578.meaning: You find freedom by knowing your true self and uniting with that truth.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10578.context: The self finds freedom by recognizing its own true nature and unity.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10579.meaning: The eternal truth is pure and original, and it is the only real thing.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10579.context: The king is told the eternal truth is pure and original, beyond envy.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10580.meaning: Understand the true difference between people to help others find their own path.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10580.context: The king is advised to understand the difference between the faithful and others.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10552.meaning: True awakening comes from understanding the invisible reality that holds everything together in the universe.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10552.context: Sages discuss how people wake up to the hidden truth that cannot be seen.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10553.meaning: The ultimate divine reality is too vast to be fully grasped by limited human thoughts or numbers.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10553.context: A father teaches his son that the highest truth is beyond simple mental counting.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10554.meaning: Understanding the fundamental building blocks of life helps you see the eternal truth behind all things.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10554.context: Teachers explain the core nature of reality and the twenty-five basic elements of existence.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10555.meaning: True awakening comes from understanding the invisible reality that holds everything together in the universe.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10555.context: Sages discuss how people wake up to the hidden truth that cannot be seen.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10557.meaning: Understanding the fundamental building blocks of life helps you see the eternal truth behind all things.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10557.context: Teachers explain the core nature of reality and the twenty-five basic elements of existence.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10558.meaning: True awakening comes from understanding the invisible reality that holds everything together in the universe.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10558.context: Sages discuss how people wake up to the hidden truth that cannot be seen.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10559.meaning: The ultimate divine reality is too vast to be fully grasped by limited human thoughts or numbers.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10559.context: A father teaches his son that the highest truth is beyond simple mental counting.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10560.meaning: True awakening comes from understanding the invisible reality that holds everything together in the universe.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10560.context: Sages discuss how people wake up to the hidden truth that cannot be seen.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10655.meaning: God created the space between limits to hold the world together and keep everything in its proper place.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10655.context: The text names a king and describes how the Lord shaped the middle sky between two limits.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10656.meaning: Time is vast and cyclical, reminding us that our lives are small parts of a much bigger eternal story.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10656.context: Scholars count time in huge cycles called kalpas, describing the long night of the universe's rest.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10657.meaning: Our sense of self and spirit come from deep roots, showing that we are all connected to ancient wisdom.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10657.context: A wise sage created ego and divine beings, giving birth to fourteen sons who became fathers of others.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10658.meaning: Living creatures are special and valued, teaching us to respect all life forms as part of the divine plan.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10658.context: Gods and ancestral daughters filled the worlds, and we hear that moving beings are the best of all.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10659.meaning: Rest and pause are natural parts of life, helping us understand that even the universe needs time to recover.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10659.context: The text describes a specific night of rest, counting five thousand kalpas as a long period of time.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10661.meaning: Our senses help us experience the world, so we should use them to appreciate the beauty around us daily.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10661.context: The five senses of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are listed as key features of living beings.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10662.meaning: We often mix love with rivalry, so we should try to support others without letting pride or jealousy win.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10662.context: People care for each other but also compete, feeling proud and jealous of one another in their daily lives.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10663.meaning: Life is full of change and loss, teaching us to accept that everything in nature is always moving and shifting.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10663.context: Animals in the universe change and die due to the strong virtues and endless losses of other beings.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10841.meaning: True power stays calm and still while it guides the busy and changing world around us every day.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10841.context: The text describes how motion causes creation while the creator remains still and unmoved in the background.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10842.meaning: Spiritual growth is an endless journey where we keep moving forward toward truth without ever stopping.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10842.context: Two eternal forces are described as endless and always moving toward a higher spiritual goal together.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10843.meaning: True wisdom is pure and never gets dirty or tired no matter how much you share it with others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10843.context: The infinite source creates life endlessly without being used up or corrupted by the process of birth.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10844.meaning: Understanding that nature works on its own helps us see the hidden truth behind every action we take.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10844.context: Wise people say nature acts endlessly because it is the doer of all actions in the world.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10845.meaning: Doing your daily work with focus and care brings real value and connects you to deeper spiritual truths.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10845.context: Daily actions filled with knowledge create wealth and connect us to the deep wisdom of the Vedas.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10846.meaning: Reading books is not enough unless you truly understand the deep lessons and apply them to your life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10846.context: Those who do not understand the true meaning of the scriptures are said to not truly know them.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10847.meaning: Memorizing rules is useless if you do not truly understand the simple truth that lies behind those rules.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10847.context: Studying many texts with rituals does not guarantee knowledge if the heart does not grasp the truth.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10848.meaning: Work hard and stay focused to find the best results without wasting time or energy on useless things.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10848.context: The text uses the metaphor of churning milk to find butter, warning against waste and slowness in effort.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10900.meaning: Even though God is invisible, showing respect at sacred places helps your heart grow closer to the divine truth.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10900.context: The divine reality is hidden from view. Wise people should still visit holy sites and perform rituals with respect.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10901.meaning: You cannot buy spiritual truth with effort alone. You must understand the hidden reality with your own mind.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10901.context: Studying books or doing hard tasks does not reveal the hidden truth. Only true inner knowing brings you there.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10902.meaning: Let go of your pride and self importance. True peace comes when you stop thinking only about yourself.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10902.context: The mind often feels like a big ego. You must move past this selfish pride to find peace.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10903.meaning: The soul is eternal and pure. It exists beyond the temporary cycles of life, death, and moral choices.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10903.context: Scripture lovers know a truth that lasts forever. It is separate from birth, death, good, and bad.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10904.meaning: True understanding helps you escape the cycle of rebirth. Rituals alone cannot free your soul from suffering.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10904.context: Ancient kings passed down this wisdom. Knowledge is better than rituals for crossing the barrier of life.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10905.meaning: Rituals offer only temporary rewards. True freedom requires wisdom to escape the endless cycle of life and death.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10905.context: Birth and death are like a strong fortress. Rituals may give temporary heaven, but you fall back down.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10906.meaning: Dedicate your daily actions to the divine. This pure worship transforms you into a wise and liberated person.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10906.context: Worship the supreme truth and Shiva. Use earthly knowledge as a sacrifice to become a wise sage.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10907.meaning: Ancient wisdom teaches us to live wisely. Following these teachings leads to lasting peace and spiritual freedom.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10907.context: King Janaka and Yajnavalkya wrote the Upanishads. They teach how to spend life wisely for eternal peace.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10941.meaning: Leaders often seek wisdom from travelers, showing that true knowledge comes from those who have seen much.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10941.context: A king asks a wandering sage where he has been and where he is heading next.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10942.meaning: True virtue takes time to grow, and we must look to wise elders for guidance on living well.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10942.context: The sage explains that goodness is hard to find early in life or during the birth age.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10943.meaning: Real greatness comes from inner strength, not outer displays, and we should value humility over status.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10943.context: The sage says he does not need fancy items like umbrellas and wants to show his respect.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10944.meaning: Knowing your teachers and roots helps you understand your own path and honor the wisdom you have received.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10944.context: The old man identifies himself as a respected disciple of a famous monk named Panchashikha.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10945.meaning: Different paths can lead to freedom, and studying them helps clear confusion and bring peace to the mind.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10945.context: The sage lists various spiritual practices like Sankhya and Yoga that help cut through doubt.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10947.meaning: Following ancient rules can bring simple joy, and a steady routine helps us find contentment in daily life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10947.context: He describes wandering along scriptural paths and living happily for four months during the year.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10948.meaning: You can find inner freedom without leaving your home, and true peace is available right where you stand.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10948.context: The sage claims to be Sankhya and speaks of liberation while staying within the kingdom.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10949.meaning: Letting go of strong desires allows you to stand firm in truth and reach a state of deep calm.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10949.context: He describes himself as free from passion and standing alone at the highest spiritual step.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10966.meaning: Real understanding of truth is the only key that can truly set your spirit free forever.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10966.context: A wise teacher asks if true knowledge alone frees a person from the cycle of life.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10967.meaning: Small comforts like soft flowers are just distractions and do not help you reach spiritual freedom.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10967.context: The speaker compares soft lotus flowers to temporary comforts that do not lead to true freedom.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10968.meaning: Knowing the truth is what frees you, not your body or the pain you feel right now.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10968.context: The text argues that knowing the truth matters more than any physical condition or state of being.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10970.meaning: Seeking comfort from pain is like using an umbrella, which is a temporary fix, not a real solution.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10970.context: The mind seeks relief from pain, similar to how people use umbrellas to avoid the rain.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10971.meaning: When you are deeply asleep, you are free from worry, but knowledge frees you while awake.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10971.context: The text explains that deep unconsciousness is a state of freedom, while waking life brings bondage.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10972.meaning: Money, power, and strong desires are chains, so I choose to stay free from all of them.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10972.context: The speaker sees wealth, power, and desire as traps that keep the soul bound to the world.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10973.meaning: I am free now, so please listen to my words about the illusions that trap most people.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10973.context: A liberated teacher tells a monk to listen carefully to the nature of what is not real.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10975.meaning: Focusing on looks, age, and body care is not the right way to find true inner peace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_10975.context: The speaker questions if physical beauty, youth, and body care are the true rules for spiritual life.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11345.meaning: Wisdom acts like a bright lamp that helps you see your true self clearly inside.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11345.context: The text compares a dark house to the mind, showing how light reveals hidden things.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11347.meaning: True wisdom means seeing the whole truth and knowing exactly what is needed for life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11347.context: A student speaks to a wise teacher, acknowledging that the teacher sees everything perfectly.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11348.meaning: A good teacher guides you to the end of all questions through their kind help.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11348.context: A devotee praises a great sage for reaching the highest level of spiritual understanding.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11349.meaning: God's grace helps you understand deep truths that you could not find on your own.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11349.context: The speaker explains that divine grace allows the sage to reveal deep spiritual truths.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11350.meaning: You may know many things but still miss the true value of what you already have.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11350.context: The text notes that people often have much knowledge but fail to see their real worth.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11351.meaning: Fear and doubt can stop you from finding peace, even if you learn new things.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11351.context: The verse lists common human problems like fear and doubt that block spiritual progress.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11352.meaning: Sincere faith and time can remove inner knots and help you find the right path.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11352.context: A person says that pure devotion and age help cut away doubt and open the heart.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11353.meaning: You need a calm mind and pure knowledge to reach the highest spiritual state.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11353.context: The text discusses how steady intellect and pure knowledge are needed to reach the divine.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11809.meaning: True wisdom often comes from a place beyond what our normal eyes can see or understand.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11809.context: The heroes could not see the man because his light was too bright for them.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11810.meaning: Beautiful and pure people often stand out clearly in a crowd because of their inner goodness.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11810.context: At the wedding, the group saw men who looked like the moon and had special marks.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11812.meaning: Deep focus and prayer can make even simple creatures feel the power of the divine.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11812.context: Great souls chanted sacred words with full focus while a monkey watched them closely.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11813.meaning: True strength and brightness can shine through even in the hardest or most difficult times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11813.context: A woman was described as strong and bright, like a tiger among holy men at the end of time.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11814.meaning: We often look for one single source of power, but true greatness is shared by all.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11814.context: They thought the island was the home of a great god named Tejo who was the most powerful.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11815.meaning: Sudden moments of great clarity can reveal the truth that was hidden before.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11815.context: A bright light like a thousand suns appeared, and then they saw Jupiter again.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11816.meaning: Important spiritual duties can be lost or changed if we are not careful and attentive.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11816.context: They heard a loud noise as men spoke about a sacrifice being taken away by others.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11818.meaning: When we face something truly great, our normal senses may fail us completely.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11818.context: The heroes were overwhelmed by the brilliance and could not see or sense anything around them.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11800.meaning: Hard work and focus can create extraordinary results, showing that dedication brings powerful outcomes.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11800.context: Four thousand years of strict practices led to perfect wooden beings standing on one foot, gathered together.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11801.meaning: True living comes from inner awareness, not external surroundings, and sharing this with others strengthens community.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11801.context: A bridegroom’s voice speaks to ascetic Brahmins, urging them to live in a well-burnt place with inner self.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11803.meaning: The divine is visible when we look beyond physical world, seeing light and purity in spiritual truth.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11803.context: Devotees ask how to see the Supreme Lord, described as a bright white island north of a salt ocean.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11804.meaning: Spiritual practice leads to inner peace, and the highest goal is to become one with the divine.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11804.context: Narayana shines like the moon; devotees reach solitude, praised as the supreme human being.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11805.meaning: True devotion removes worldly cravings, allowing one to experience pure, fragrant presence of the divine.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11805.context: They enter the eternal God of a thousand flames, becoming transcendental, hungry, unaware, and fragrant.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11806.meaning: Solitude and sharing wisdom help reveal deeper truths about the soul to those who seek it.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11806.context: Men live alone on Shaveta island; sages are invited, and the soul is revealed to others.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11807.meaning: Guidance from higher realms can direct us back to our roots, showing the importance of following wise paths.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11807.context: A disembodied voice is heard; people return to their country following a described route.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11808.meaning: Sometimes what we expect to find is not pleasant, reminding us to prepare for unexpected outcomes.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_11808.context: Reaching the white continent, he wanted to see it, but the sight was repulsive.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_12311.meaning: Shows how powerful beings can have both fearsome and attractive features, teaching balance.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_12_12311.context: Describes a creature with many teeth, fangs, and a beautiful face in a mythic story.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1185.meaning: Rest and comfort are gifts we should accept graciously when offered by kind and generous hosts.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1185.context: She sits on a bright bed and tells the guest to rest while horses pass by.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1186.meaning: Spiritual conversations can illuminate the mind and bring a sense of peace to the soul.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1186.context: The brahmin talks with her and lies down on a second bed that shines with divine light.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1187.meaning: Sharing knowledge and warmth helps others feel safe and cared for during difficult or cold times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1187.context: She shivers from the cold, and the sage teaches her before they both go to sleep.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1686.meaning: Respect sages and seek their guidance. Recognizing righteousness, Bhrigu leaves after worshiping Dharmaraja, who inquires about his visit.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1686.context: Bhrigu, a sage, recognizes Dharmaraja and leaves the hermitage after worshiping him. The king asks why Bhrigu came.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1687.meaning: Ask for knowledge and wisdom from wise individuals. Dharmaraja seeks clarification on Bhrigu's visit, showing curiosity and respect.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1687.context: King Dharmaraja inquires about Bhrigu's visit and the reason behind it.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1688.meaning: Understand the consequences of past actions. Bhrigu informs Dharmaraja about the kingdom's peril because of his family's wicked actions in the past.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1688.context: Bhrigu explains that the king's kingdom is in danger due to his own lineage's evil deeds.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1689.meaning: Seek guidance from wise individuals to rectify past mistakes and protect one's kingdom. Dharmaraja, influenced by Bhrigu's advice, takes action to safeguard the kingdom and turns to sages for assistance.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1689.context: Dharmaraja, moved by Bhrigu's words, decides to protect the kingdom and seek the help of sages.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1690.meaning: Seek guidance from knowledgeable individuals to rectify wrongdoings and protect the realm. Bhrigu instructs Dharmaraja to eliminate the evil family to safeguard the kingdom.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1690.context: Bhrigu advises Dharmaraja to protect the kingdom by destroying the wicked lineage.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1691.meaning: Accept advice from wise individuals and act upon it for the betterment of the realm. Dharmaraja agrees to Bhrigu's suggestion and seeks his blessings for the noble endeavor.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1691.context: Dharmaraja agrees to destroy the wicked lineage and seeks the blessings of Bhrigu.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1692.meaning: Seek guidance from wise individuals and act upon it for the betterment of the realm. Bhrigu blesses Dharmaraja for his decision to rectify the kingdom's problems.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1692.context: Bhrigu blesses Dharmaraja for his decision to eliminate the wicked lineage.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1693.meaning: Understand the impact of actions and prioritize kingdom protection. Dharmaraja, realizing the outcomes of his decisions, chooses to safeguard the realm.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_1693.context: Dharmaraja, understanding the consequences of his actions, decides to protect the kingdom.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2114.meaning: A daughter holds equal value to a son in family matters and deserves the same respect and inheritance rights.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2114.context: The text discusses how wealth is measured and states that a daughter deserves respect like a son.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2115.meaning: When a person stays true to their inner self, no one can take away their true worth or dignity.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2115.context: The verse explains that a daughter is equal to a son and her inner self protects her wealth.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2116.meaning: A daughter has the right to claim her share of family property when her father cannot provide for her.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2116.context: This part talks about the mother's dowry and how a daughter might claim rights if the father lacks them.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2117.meaning: Righteousness demands that sons and daughters share equally in the inheritance left by their parents and grandparents.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2117.context: The text says there is no difference between sons and daughters when it comes to inheriting ancestral property.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2118.meaning: A daughter who stays close to home is often more valuable than a son who lives far away.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2118.context: The verse compares a daughter to a son born elsewhere, suggesting the daughter is often preferred in certain contexts.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2119.meaning: A righteous daughter brings honor to the family, while sons who are sold do not carry the same weight.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2119.context: The speaker sees no fault in the daughter's righteousness and mentions sons who are sold or given away.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2120.meaning: People who act with jealousy and deceit are like demons because they break the rules of right and good behavior.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2120.context: The text describes people who are jealous, deceitful, and act against righteousness, comparing them to demons.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2121.meaning: Even gods of justice follow strict moral laws, showing that everyone must live by the rules of righteousness.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2121.context: Scholars recite stories of Yama, the god of justice, who knew righteousness and was bound by sacred laws.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2282.meaning: True peace comes from mastering your own emotions and letting go of ego and anger.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2282.context: A wise man lived alone in the river for twelve years to control his feelings.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2284.meaning: Respect every living being because the divine spirit shines through all creatures on earth.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2284.context: The sage held a deep belief that all living things are connected to the divine.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2285.meaning: Humility and purity of heart allow you to connect deeply with the divine power.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2285.context: The sage became very pure and bowed to the gods while water flowed around him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2286.meaning: Stay calm and focused even when life feels chaotic, loud, or moves very fast.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2286.context: The fast moving rivers made a loud noise, but the sage stayed calm and steady.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2287.meaning: When you live with respect and peace, the world around you becomes supportive and kind.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2287.context: The rivers followed the sage and gave him gifts without causing him any harm.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2288.meaning: Resting in silence and stillness can help you gain deep inner wisdom and understanding.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2288.context: The sage slept deep in the water and woke up with new wisdom and clarity.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2289.meaning: A peaceful and pure presence brings joy and comfort to everyone around you.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2289.context: Fish and other water creatures saw the sage and felt happy to be near him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2290.meaning: Sometimes ordinary people enter sacred spaces, showing that the divine is everywhere in life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2290.context: Fishermen arrived at that spot with their nets, ready to catch fish in the water.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2869.meaning: Living in a community that respects nature and wise teachers brings peace and protection to everyone.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2869.context: The text describes a holy place where cows drink water and people respect wise leaders.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2870.meaning: If you stay steady and strong inside, you will not be broken by the hard times in life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2870.context: This verse talks about a person who stays strong and calm even when life gets very hard.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2871.meaning: Showing respect to divine forces with simple gifts helps you connect with the spiritual world.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2871.context: The text lists several important gods and says they are honored with offerings of butter.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2872.meaning: Giving pure and simple gifts to the divine is the best way to heal your spirit.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2872.context: The speaker calls a specific offering the best medicine, sacrifice, juice, and fruit for the soul.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2873.meaning: Instead of chasing selfish wants, you should share your best resources with the divine for peace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2873.context: People always want fame and food, but the text says pure people should give butter to gods.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2875.meaning: Sharing food with the divine creates a shield of safety and peace for your family and home.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2875.context: The verse says that offering sweet food mixed with butter to gods protects the home from harm.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2876.meaning: When you give generously to others, you will never lack for what you truly need in life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2876.context: The text describes a person who is never thirsty and is seen with many good things around him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2877.meaning: Living a pure life brings you close to the divine and gives you a special blessing.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_2877.context: The verse mentions a man who is accompanied by supreme autumn and receives a special touch.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3719.meaning: Peaceful listening helps us learn important traditions and respect the past.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3719.context: Yudhisthira talks to Bhishma, who then lives peacefully and explains autumn rituals.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3720.meaning: Honoring sacrifices brings good reputation and protects against enemies.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3720.context: A king is asked to listen to a blessed autumn ceremony about fame and sacrifice.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3721.meaning: All living beings deserve respect, showing humility and unity in worship.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3721.context: The verse lists many beings, gods, demons, humans, and others, who are worshipped.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3722.meaning: Complete devotion to ancestors and gods brings harmony and blessings.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3722.context: After honoring ancestors, people please the gods, so everyone should worship fully.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3723.meaning: Following proper rituals honors ancestors and keeps traditions alive.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3723.context: A king is told about a special ancestor ritual called Sharaddhama, involving meat.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3724.meaning: Regular offerings show respect and keep family bonds strong.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3724.context: Grandfathers are pleased by daily autumn offerings, and the speaker will explain them.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3725.meaning: Doing good deeds on sacred days brings positive results.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3725.context: A sinless person receives rewards from arrows given on special days, and the speaker will explain.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3814.meaning: Choosing the right time for rituals matters, and we should avoid selfish motives in our actions.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3814.context: A sage decides to perform a ritual called Sharaddha at a specific time, but feels selfish.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3815.meaning: We should seek guidance from higher powers when making important choices.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3815.context: The speaker asks the lord to listen as autumn begins and he shares his decision.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3817.meaning: Strong spiritual leaders inspire others and leave lasting legacies.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3817.context: The great sage Dattatreya is remembered for his power and lineage among the Kauravas.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3818.meaning: Spiritual practice can be passed down through families, strengthening devotion.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3818.context: Dattatreya’s son Nimira was a devoted ascetic, and Nimira’s son Sharima lived with discipline.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3819.meaning: True devotion endures through time and leads to peace even in death.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3819.context: After a thousand years, a man performed hard austerities and faced death with righteousness.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3820.meaning: Rituals help us cope with grief and honor those we love.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3820.context: Nimis performed purification rituals and mourned deeply for his son.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3821.meaning: Dedication to rituals can bring clarity even in difficult times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3821.context: The wise man offered sacrifices on the fourteenth day and woke up during darkness.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3822.meaning: Grief can sharpen our thoughts and help us understand what truly matters.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_3822.context: He woke again, his soul full of grief, and his mind focused on the object of sorrow.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4104.meaning: All good things come from nature, and we should thank the divine for providing nourishment.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4104.context: A poem about nature's gifts, trees, herbs, and rain, praising the Lord for all food.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4105.meaning: Life's important events are celebrated with rituals that honor the gods and bring blessings.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4105.context: Describes many ceremonies: births, weddings, cattle rituals, and sacrifices for prosperity.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4106.meaning: Giving and sharing help others, and food reminds us to be generous and kind.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4106.context: Talks about meetings, donations, and sharing money, encouraged by food and the sage Bhrigu.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4107.meaning: True beauty and new starts come from deeper values, not just from eating.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4107.context: Speaks of beauty and new beginnings, saying everything goes beyond food and is known.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4108.meaning: We should not compare ourselves; the sun shines for everyone, not just for one person.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4108.context: A Brahmin asks why the sun shines on others first, while he feels overlooked.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4109.meaning: Seeking answers from higher powers helps us understand our actions and their results.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4109.context: An ascetic asks the sun what powerful Jamadagni did to return to him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4110.meaning: Respect and humility earn the sun's favor and the blessings of the world.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4110.context: The sun replies in a gentle tone, bowing to a humble Brahmin with folded hands.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4112.meaning: Understanding truth and staying humble bring peace and wisdom in daily life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4112.context: The speaker says he knows the steady or moving truth, and he will be humble today.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4271.meaning: True goodness protects people from harm. Do not doubt the power of virtue and divine grace in life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4271.context: Sages defend a holy man who survived fire and was not cursed by other wise leaders.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4272.meaning: Past kindness creates lasting bonds. We should honor those who have received divine gifts and blessings.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4272.context: Speakers remind the lord that he gave nectar before, so they will not harm this great soul.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4273.meaning: Do not use power to hurt others. Causing pain through selfish wishes makes you the lowest of men.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4273.context: A speaker warns against granting boons that cause grief, calling such acts unrighteous against the gods.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4274.meaning: Listen with an open heart. Being willing to learn and follow wise advice leads to better outcomes.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4274.context: A listener asks the speaker to share what remains, promising to follow the instructions given.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4275.meaning: Pride can lead to conflict. Remember that strength without humility often brings trouble and downfall.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4275.context: A speaker arrives on behalf of his proud grandfather Nahusha, who was strong and fought back.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4276.meaning: Arrogance leads to humiliation. Even powerful leaders can be brought low by their own bad choices.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4276.context: A speaker declares that the king of gods will be yoked to a chariot today by Indra's power.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4277.meaning: Justice restores order. Righteous actions remove evil influences and bring back peace and proper leadership.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4277.context: Indra will be installed while watching sacrifices, removing him from a place of evil-minded people.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4278.meaning: Fate humbles the proud. When ego blinds us, we destroy ourselves by ignoring wisdom and truth.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4278.context: The proud one will attack the lord's feet today because fate overwhelms his mind and destroys him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4672.meaning: Enduring hardship with patience brings immense spiritual rewards and lasting happiness in the afterlife for the soul.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4672.context: A person who fasts while suffering or old age finds great joy in heaven for a long time.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4673.meaning: Righteous people enjoy heavenly pleasures and companionship after living a life of honor and virtue on earth.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4673.context: A noble warrior shines brightly like the moon while riding a chariot pulled by many white swans.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4674.meaning: Different remedies suit different needs, so we must choose actions that heal our specific physical or mental state.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4674.context: Weak people drink and climb, while heat helps the old and food calms the angry mind.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4675.meaning: Seeking only pleasure ignores the value of duty, so true peace comes from accepting life's necessary hardships.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4675.context: Paying debts through suffering is not pleasing to those who seek only happiness and desire all of heaven.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4676.meaning: Heavenly rewards include beauty and joy, but these pleasures are tied to the desires one held in life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4676.context: A man rides a golden chariot driven by desire, while a woman enjoys crowds and wears auspicious decorations.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4677.meaning: Living a clean and focused life allows for a peaceful death and the attainment of spiritual goals.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4677.context: A healthy and pure person leaves the body without eating, achieving success and happiness in their final moments.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4678.meaning: Spiritual merit brings celebration and companionship in the afterlife, reflecting the joy earned through good deeds.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4678.context: Divine bells ring and flags wave as a man grows happier while being followed by a thousand women.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4680.meaning: Every small part of our being contributes to our spiritual reward, so even tiny good deeds matter greatly.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4680.context: The number of years a person rejoices in heaven equals the number of hair follicles on their limbs.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4918.meaning: The importance of leading a virtuous life and overcoming evil to achieve a better rebirth as a human being.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4918.context: In Hinduism, this verse from the Mahabharata talks about the cycle of life and rebirth. It mentions a worm living for fifteen years after destroying evil, and then being reborn as a human being.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4919.meaning: Engaging in religious rituals doesn't guarantee happiness or a long life. Satisfaction comes from inner peace and living a virtuous life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4919.context: The verse describes a ritual performed by a person, who is still not satisfied and is reborn as a crow after ten years.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4920.meaning: Harming or neglecting family members, especially elder brothers and equals, can lead to negative karma and a poor rebirth. Treating others with respect and kindness is important for a better life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4920.context: This verse from the Mahabharata talks about the consequences of treating one's elder brother and equal to one's father, which leads to rebirth in the Karaunchayonas after death.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4921.meaning: Serving others and leading a virtuous life can lead to positive karma and a better rebirth. The cycle of life and rebirth is based on one's actions and intentions.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4921.context: In Hinduism, this verse from the Mahabharata explains how a bull gives birth to two worms after serving a Brahmin, and then the worms give birth to a mouse after ten years.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4922.meaning: Good actions result in good karma and a better rebirth. Evil actions lead to negative karma and a poor rebirth. Choosing righteousness is crucial for a better existence.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4922.context: The importance of leading a virtuous life.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4923.meaning: Living a good life ensures a better rebirth. Neglecting virtues leads to a cycle of suffering and rebirth in lower forms of life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4923.context: The verse from the Mahabharata talks about the cycle of life and rebirth, emphasizing the importance of leading a virtuous life.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4924.meaning: Good actions result in positive karma and a better rebirth. Evil actions lead to negative karma and a poor rebirth. Doing righteous deeds is essential for a better existence.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4924.context: This verse from the Mahabharata discusses the cycle of life and rebirth, highlighting the consequences of one's actions.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4925.meaning: Living a virtuous life ensures a better rebirth. Engaging in sinful deeds leads to suffering and rebirth in lower forms of life. Pursuing righteousness is vital for a superior existence.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_4925.context: The verse from the Mahabharata talks about the cycle of life and rebirth, emphasizing the importance of leading a virtuous life.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5299.meaning: Being closed off to good advice causes inner stress. Open your heart to learn and find peace instead of anger.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5299.context: A wise speaker addresses a stubborn person who refuses to listen to advice or change their mind.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5300.meaning: Chasing selfish goals drains your energy. Let go of attachment to results and find true freedom in your actions.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5300.context: The speaker points out that the listener is driven by selfish desires and attachments to specific outcomes.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5301.meaning: True friendship involves honest feedback. Accept the truth about yourself to grow stronger and heal your spirit.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5301.context: A friend speaks honestly about the other person's virtues while pointing out their current frail state.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5302.meaning: Hiding your true self causes weakness. Be honest about your motives to build inner strength and confidence.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5302.context: The listener hides their true intentions out of shame, leading to a weak and fragile condition.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5303.meaning: Seeking approval from others drains you. Focus on inner wisdom and character rather than external praise or fame.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5303.context: The speaker criticizes the listener for seeking fame from others instead of focusing on inner knowledge.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5305.meaning: Unfulfilled desires and feeling exploited cause suffering. Find contentment within yourself rather than relying on external gains.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5305.context: The listener has not achieved their long desired goals and feels used or taken advantage of.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5306.meaning: Feeling unjustly judged causes deep stress. Reflect on your actions calmly and do not let false accusations break you.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5306.context: The listener feels unfairly criticized because they believe they have done nothing wrong in their life.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5307.meaning: Suffering without purpose drains the soul. Seek meaning in your struggles and protect your inner peace from harm.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5307.context: The speaker describes a situation where friendly people suffer harm without any meaningful virtue or reason.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6004.meaning: Fear can arise from hearing wise words, but the wind reminds us to stay calm and listen.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6004.context: Arjuna speaks, nightwalker feels scared, wind speaks in the open air.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6006.meaning: Keeping bad thoughts inside harms everyone; sharing them with wise people helps cleanse the nation.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6006.context: Offer dirty thoughts to Brahmins, sin causes trouble for the whole country.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6008.meaning: Even in scary moments, the wind (spirit) can guide us to calm and understanding.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6008.context: Arjuna talks, nightwalker is frightened, wind speaks in the open space.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6009.meaning: A messenger can bring good news, showing that help comes from caring voices.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6009.context: The king asks who is speaking, the messenger says he speaks for the king’s good.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6012.meaning: Showing love to wise people helps us see how the world changes for the better.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6012.context: Today you show devotion to Brahmins, ask what the earth has become.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6013.meaning: Use simple, pure words like water or sun to share clear, bright ideas.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6013.context: Write like Vayor or a great Brahmin, compare to water or sun.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6014.meaning: Heed wise names; they guide the king and show the best path for everyone.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6014.context: Listen, fool, to the good names of Brahmins, king, Brahmin is best.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6015.meaning: Leaving power can lead to conflict; fear and destruction show the danger of losing respect.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6015.context: He left the earth’s kingdom, fought king of Anga, Brahmin feared, was destroyed.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6453.meaning: Respecting leaders and communities builds trust and shows humility, encouraging cooperation and harmony.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6453.context: A king visits Varanasi, meeting citizens, ministers, and elders, showing respect to the city’s leaders.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6454.meaning: Celebrating new life with gratitude strengthens family bonds and honors cultural traditions.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6454.context: The king’s son is born in Paurajanapada, celebrated with worship before returning home.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6456.meaning: Comforting the lost and rewarding kindness encourages compassion and generosity in society.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6456.context: The lord comforts fallen heroes and gods, then the king gives him many chariots.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6457.meaning: Wise leadership and organized governance bring stability and prosperity for everyone.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6457.context: Yudhisthira is crowned, gaining the kingdom, and the best men organize all subjects.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6458.meaning: Unity among leaders and followers creates a strong, righteous community that thrives together.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6458.context: Brahmins, army chiefs, and Naigamas support the righteous chief, who receives blessings.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6459.meaning: Reflecting on history teaches lessons, helping people avoid past mistakes and grow wiser.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6459.context: People stay overnight in fifty-eight cities, remembering the Kaurava leader’s past.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6460.meaning: Traveling with guidance and observing nature reminds us to stay humble and mindful.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6460.context: Surrounded by priests, he leaves Gajapura, watching the sunset and northern light.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6461.meaning: Giving gifts shows respect and gratitude, fostering goodwill and strong relationships.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6461.context: Yudhisthira offers ghee, garlands, fragrances, silk, sandalwood, and black agaru to chiefs.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_11.meaning: Strike when your opponent is weak to destroy their power and win the fight decisively.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_11.context: Krisha tells Bhima to grab the enemy who is weak and suffering during the battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_12.meaning: Stay alert and focused so you never miss the moment when evil finally falls.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_12.context: Krisha asks two warriors to watch him closely so they do not miss the enemy's defeat.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_14.meaning: A good leader who follows moral rules will bring peace and order to the land.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_14.context: The text says to crown Yudhisthira as king because he is good and follows the right path.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_15.meaning: May wisdom and life grow in all people, and may your family keep learning and thriving.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_15.context: A prayer asks the divine presence to be in all people and help the royal line grow.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_17.meaning: Following bad choices leads to empty regret, so always choose the right and honest path.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_17.context: Vidura writes to Duryodhana that he followed wrong paths and gained nothing but regret.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_18.meaning: Even brave beings feel deep sorrow when they lose loved ones or face painful endings.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_18.context: A speaker mourns a brave horse that died after hearing sweet words and facing great pain.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_19.meaning: Do not let sadness control you, especially when your elders are also feeling the pain.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_19.context: Speakers tell the king that his old fathers are sad and he should stop feeling sorry.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_20.meaning: Sometimes silence is the best response, and wise leaders know when to speak and when to listen.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_20.context: King Dhritarashtra speaks to the wise king, who then stays quiet and talks to Tama.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_52.meaning: We should show kindness to the poor and not ask for money from those who have nothing.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_52.context: The Pandavas feel sorry for poor children and see princes struggling with wet clothes.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_53.meaning: Sometimes rituals can cause great suffering, so we must think carefully before demanding heavy sacrifices.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_53.context: A king speaks to a sage about the heavy cost of a huge religious ceremony.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_54.meaning: One person's bad choices can ruin many lives and bring deep shame to an entire family.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_54.context: The Pandavas blame Duryodhana for their loss of kingdom and the great shame they face.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_55.meaning: Greed and wickedness by leaders can destroy society and cause great harm to everyone around them.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_55.context: The text says Duryodhana's greed and Dhritarashtra's bad actions destroyed the earth's balance.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_56.meaning: True justice is the foundation of society, even when the rules seem hard to understand at first.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_56.context: The text discusses how the earth represents law and how rules can seem confusing at times.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_57.meaning: You should speak for yourself honestly and let the wise person guide you with their own words.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_57.context: A speaker tells a sage that he does not want to represent anyone else in this matter.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_58.meaning: It is wise to pause and think carefully before giving an important answer to a friend.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_58.context: Krishna listens to Arjuna's request and thinks for a moment before giving his answer.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_59.meaning: Sometimes the solution to a big problem is a simple object that you just need to find.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_59.context: The sage tells Arjuna to bring a specific door from a mountain to solve a problem.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_68.meaning: Even in good families, bad behavior from one person can hurt everyone around them.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_68.context: Good brothers lived together but their oldest brother caused them much pain and trouble.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_69.meaning: Winning a title is not enough if you cannot protect the people you lead.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_69.context: A new king won the land but failed to keep the people safe and happy.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_70.meaning: Removing bad things from your life makes room for new happiness and growth.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_70.context: A wise man cleared away the darkness and welcomed his new son with joy.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_71.meaning: Seeing suffering can inspire you to focus on helping others rather than yourself.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_71.context: A son saw his father lose power and decided to help others instead of himself.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_72.meaning: People naturally follow leaders who are honest, calm, and treat everyone with respect.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_72.context: A calm and honest leader gained the trust of the people because he was kind.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_73.meaning: Doing the right thing can be hard when you face loss and strong opposition.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_73.context: A king focused on doing good, but his wealth faded and enemies attacked him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_74.meaning: Sometimes you must endure great hardship to stay true to your values and people.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_74.context: The king and his city suffered greatly because of the many enemies around them.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_75.meaning: Staying honest and fair gives you strength that no enemy can easily break.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_75.context: Enemies could not defeat the king in the forest because he was always right.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_120.meaning: He shows respect, trusting the king’s promise, and refuses to give up his life for a ritual.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_120.context: A chosen warrior speaks to the earth’s lord, saying he will not sacrifice him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_121.meaning: He chooses a higher sacrifice, showing that true devotion can be offered without harming people.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_121.context: The warrior declares he will sacrifice an immortal, not a human, and ends the ceremony.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_123.meaning: He encourages others to take responsibility, teaching that sharing duties strengthens community bonds.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_123.context: He says he will not perform a sacrifice today and asks who should do it instead.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_124.meaning: The king’s joy turns to concern, reminding us to help those in trouble even after success.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_124.context: The king Marutta feels pleased and later sees the distressed sage Narada on his way.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_125.meaning: Respectful greeting shows humility, and the sage’s words guide the king toward wise actions.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_125.context: The king meets Narada, folds his hands in ritual, and then Narada speaks.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_126.meaning: He reminds the king to reflect on his well-being and the purpose of his journey.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_126.context: Narada questions the king about his happiness and his recent travels.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_127.meaning: Seeking guidance shows humility, and the sage’s promise encourages patience and calm in leadership.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_127.context: The king asks what he should do, and Narada promises to help calm his anger.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_128.meaning: Open communication keeps everyone informed, fostering trust and cooperation in difficult times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_128.context: Narada reports the delay to the teacher and shares all details with him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_129.meaning: When you seek help from a respected guide, they may refuse, showing that not all requests are granted.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_129.context: The king goes to Brihaspati, a divine teacher, to ask for a sacrificial priest, but is not welcomed.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_130.meaning: Feeling rejected can make us doubt our purpose, but we must find inner strength to keep going.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_130.context: The king feels abandoned by his teacher, Narada, and says he no longer wants to live.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_131.meaning: Kind words can lift a weary heart, reminding us that hope can return even after hardship.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_131.context: Narada speaks to the king, trying to revive his spirit with encouraging words.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_132.meaning: Seeking help from a virtuous person can bring solutions when others refuse to assist.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_132.context: The king learns of a righteous man, Samvarta, who can help him with his sacrifice.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_133.meaning: When one path is blocked, another wise path may still lead to your goal.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_133.context: The king is advised to go to Samvarta if Brihaspati will not perform the sacrifice.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_134.meaning: Patience and faith are needed to see the results of our actions, even when they seem delayed.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_134.context: Narada encourages the king, asking when he will see the outcome of his efforts.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_135.meaning: Understanding why we feel rejected helps us decide how to respond and move forward.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_135.context: The king questions how he can act toward his teacher and why he feels abandoned.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_136.meaning: Even those who appear strange can play a useful role in society, showing hidden value.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_136.context: A madman disguises himself and travels comfortably, still serving the city of Varanasi.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_929.meaning: Everything in nature is connected. We must understand how different parts of life influence and support each other.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_929.context: The five natural forces work together in a complex web of mutual dependence and interaction.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_930.meaning: Our minds have three modes. Understanding how purity, activity, and ignorance connect helps us grow spiritually.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_930.context: Three main forces exist in nature. They are purity, passion, and darkness, which are linked.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_931.meaning: Overcoming ignorance changes our behavior. Mastering one part of ourselves transforms the rest of our character.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_931.context: When one force is mastered, the others change. Controlling darkness shifts the balance of nature.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_932.meaning: Ignorance leads to poor choices. We must recognize these dark traits to avoid making harmful mistakes.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_932.context: Darkness brings confusion and bad habits. These traits are fixed in actions driven by delusion.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_933.meaning: We are not just our urges. Recognizing this helps us see our true nature beyond simple desires.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_933.context: People often mistake their instincts for their true self. This passion drives actions in all beings.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_934.meaning: A balanced mind brings peace. Cultivating purity helps us see the world clearly and act with grace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_934.context: Purity brings light and balance to all living things. This state is calm and clear.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_935.meaning: Every action has a result. Understanding these patterns helps us make better choices for our future.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_935.context: These qualities have causes and effects. They shape our lives through various actions and results.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_936.meaning: Lack of wisdom leads to suffering. Clearing our minds of confusion allows us to do good without fear.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_936.context: Ignorance causes fear, greed, and sorrow. It ruins good deeds and creates confusion in the mind.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_937.meaning: Ignoring truth and acting with blind ignorance leads to a life filled with poor choices and spiritual darkness.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_937.context: The text describes negative traits like atheism and blindness as part of a dark nature.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_938.meaning: Being proud of what you do not know and treating others poorly shows a lack of wisdom.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_938.context: Pride in ignorance and unfriendliness are listed as foolish feelings that distort the mind.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_939.meaning: Living without moral guidance creates a heavy spirit and keeps you trapped in confusion and fear.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_939.context: Unrighteousness, sin, and darkness are described as heavy burdens that cloud the soul.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_940.meaning: Behaviors rooted in laziness and delusion prevent you from seeing the truth and living a good life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_940.context: These negative virtues are declared as Tamasic, meaning they belong to the mode of inertia.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_941.meaning: Giving up duties out of anger or jealousy is not true peace but a sign of inner turmoil.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_941.context: Renunciation mixed with pride, anger, and envy is identified as a dark behavior pattern.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_943.meaning: Doing things without purpose or giving gifts out of obligation lacks true value and spiritual merit.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_943.context: Vain beginnings and useless gifts are described as Tamasic behavior related to eating or giving.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_944.meaning: Arguing just to win and refusing to accept truth shows a closed mind and lack of grace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_944.context: Excessive arguments, intolerance, and unbelief are listed as behaviors of the dark mode.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_945.meaning: Those who follow these dark paths remain stuck in ignorance and fail to reach higher understanding.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_945.context: People who live with these sinful limits are identified as Tamasic individuals in the world.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1305.meaning: You must keep trying without stopping to overcome obstacles and reach your spiritual goals with steady effort.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1305.context: A wise person must work hard to cross life's difficult challenges and reach the other side safely.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1306.meaning: Let go of old ways that no longer serve you and move forward with new strength and purpose.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1306.context: The speaker tells the listener to abandon their current method and move forward to a new place.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1307.meaning: Your pride and confusion will stop your progress if you do not let them go completely.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1307.context: Confusion and ego act like a heavy boat that traps you and prevents you from moving forward.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1308.meaning: You must use the right method for each situation, or your efforts will fail completely and waste time.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1308.context: Using the wrong tool for the job causes failure, just like trying to sail a chariot on water.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1309.meaning: Your actions shape your reality, so be careful because what you do will clearly show its effects.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1309.context: Actions create visible results in the world, showing that every deed leaves a mark on reality.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1310.meaning: The highest truth cannot be seen or touched, so you must use your mind to understand it deeply.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1310.context: Sages describe the ultimate truth as something without physical senses, existing beyond smell, taste, form, touch, or sound.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1311.meaning: Greatness comes from the divine source, but it can turn into ego if you are not careful.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1311.context: The unmanifest source is great, and from it comes the quality of greatness, which leads to ego.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1312.meaning: When ego separates us, it creates different traits, so understanding this helps you see how the world works.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1312.context: Ego creates separation, and this division leads to the different modes or qualities that define all beings.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1402.meaning: Victory comes when righteous forces defeat those who act with pride and commit many wrong deeds against others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1402.context: The speaker boasts about defeating the enemy army and killing the proud warriors who caused so much trouble.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1403.meaning: Success often depends on using your brain and clever plans rather than just relying on physical strength alone.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1403.context: The speaker credits the listener for using smart strategies to help win the great war against Duryodhana.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1404.meaning: Bad choices lead to downfall while good deeds bring honor and lasting fame to those who do them.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1404.context: The text describes how Karna was defeated and highlights the bad actions of Sandhava during the conflict.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1405.meaning: We should support good leaders and encourage those who follow the path of truth and justice.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1405.context: The speaker plans to visit King Yudhisthira to offer support and encouragement to the righteous ruler.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1407.meaning: Showing respect to guests and acknowledging family connections helps build strong bonds and shows proper hospitality.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1407.context: The host welcomes the divine guest and mentions seeing his strong uncle Baladeva and other important relatives.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1408.meaning: Reaching a sacred place brings joy and connects you with a community that shares your spiritual goals.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1408.context: The travelers arrived in the holy city of Varanasi and joined the happy crowd of people there.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1409.meaning: Even in great palaces, leaders face their own struggles and must remain humble despite their high status.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1409.context: They entered the royal palace which looked like a divine home and saw the blind king Dhritarashtra.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1410.meaning: Standing together in difficult times shows strength and helps families support each other through loss and change.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1410.context: Many women including Gandhari and others stood together in the hall showing their unity and presence.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1559.meaning: This shows how fear and violence can make a person look very frightening and dangerous.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1559.context: A warrior sees a scary king covered in blood and wearing a long mustache.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1560.meaning: Ignoring wise advice can lead to trouble and make difficult situations come back to haunt you.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1560.context: The king ignored the brahmin's advice and a scary figure rose up again.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1561.meaning: It is a great relief to find loved ones safe when you are worried about them.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1561.context: A brahmin is happy to find his friend safe while hunting for food.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1562.meaning: We must respect our basic needs and take care of our bodies when they are hungry.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1562.context: A demigod says he must eat now because he is very hungry today.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1564.meaning: It is important to finish your duties and promises before moving on to other things.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1564.context: A king asks for time to finish his teacher's work before returning.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1565.meaning: Keeping your promises to teachers and helpers shows that you are a person of honor.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1565.context: The king promised a chariot to his teacher and gives gems to priests.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1566.meaning: Generosity and good actions make you respected and worthy of the trust of others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1566.context: The king is praised for giving gifts and being worthy of respect.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1567.meaning: Patience and timing are key when you promise to complete a task or duty.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1567.context: The king promises to return to his duties in the proper time.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1678.meaning: Past hurts can fuel your strength, but true power comes from rising above old pain.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1678.context: Darona led five armies and remembered how his father had rejected him before this fight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1679.meaning: When many strong people join together, the conflict becomes overwhelming and hard to escape.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1679.context: Many princes and wise leaders gathered from different lands to fight in this huge war.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1680.meaning: Even the strongest people can be defeated if they do not take time to rest.
