hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1680.context: The battle raged for five days, and Darona finally got too tired to keep fighting.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1681.meaning: A good leader stands firm and protects their side even when the odds are against them.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1681.context: Karna led the army for Duryodhana and fought bravely with five strong groups of soldiers.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1682.meaning: Hardships in life can prepare you for great challenges, but many will not survive the struggle.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1682.context: The three sons of Pandu were raised in hard places, and many heroes fell in battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1683.meaning: Sometimes we are drawn to danger or destruction because we cannot see the clear path.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1683.context: One warrior moved toward Partha like a moth to a flame on the second day of war.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1684.meaning: Doing the right thing often requires great effort and courage, even when it is hard.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1684.context: Yudhisthira, the king, killed the king of Madras in a very difficult and fierce fight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1687.meaning: Quick action and strong skills can save the day when someone tries to steal your victory.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1687.context: Shalya killed a bird, and Sahadeva used his great skill to stop the one taking it away.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_39.meaning: Parents often love their children deeply and ignore their flaws because they want them to succeed in life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_39.context: King Dhritarashtra looks at his blind sons and feels happy because he sees no bad signs in them.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_40.meaning: Seeing others do good can sometimes make us feel proud of our own family instead of humble.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_40.context: The good behavior of the Pandavas makes King Dhritarashtra feel proud of his own sons who are present.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_41.meaning: True leadership means treating everyone with kindness and care even if they are your rivals or foes.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_41.context: The mothers comfort their sons and the king treats his enemies as if they were his own children.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_42.meaning: People often defend their own group and believe their leader is strong and right in all things.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_42.context: The speaker says the Kauravas are not bad and the king acts with great strength and royal power.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_43.meaning: A good partner respects the other person and values their opinion in every decision they make together.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_43.context: King Dhritarashtra listens to his wife Gandhari and follows her advice on all matters big or small.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_44.meaning: Respecting others words and knowing when to step back shows true strength and wisdom in conflict.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_44.context: The mighty warrior of the Pandavas honors the words spoken and then withdraws from the situation calmly.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_45.meaning: People often use prayer and ritual to ask for protection and health for the ones they love most.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_45.context: The king performs sacred rituals and offers sacrifices to the fire to pray for his sons long life.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_48.meaning: Society works best when all groups respect each other and live together in harmony without fighting or hate.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_48.context: Brahmins elders warriors and common people all lived together in peace and were loved by everyone then.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_256.meaning: Great leaders often come together to discuss important matters and seek guidance from those who hold wisdom and authority.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_256.context: Many wise priests and powerful kings gathered from far away lands to meet the blind king Dhritarashtra.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_266.meaning: We should recognize our true identity and accept our circumstances with grace, finding peace even in difficult or wild places.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_266.context: A speaker identifies himself as a blind son named Kagati and addresses fortunate listeners about their place in the forest.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_267.meaning: When everyone listens with a calm and focused mind, we can understand important truths that unite different groups of people.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_267.context: Priests and people from all social classes gathered in the forest and listened with focused and serious attention.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_268.meaning: Seeking counsel from respected elders and leaders is a wise way to navigate complex situations and find the right path.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_268.context: Priests and kings arrived from many different countries to stand before the mighty and blind king Dhritarashtra.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_269.meaning: A leader succeeds when supported by loyal helpers who bring strength and good reputation to the community.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_269.context: King Shantanu ruled the earth well because Bhishma supported him with great strength and a famous reputation for skill.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_270.meaning: When we treat loved ones with kindness and respect, they remain cherished and safe in our hearts and homes.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_270.context: The speaker mentions his white brother who became beloved and was treated with care and respect by everyone.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_271.meaning: Pride and bad intentions lead to serious conflict, so we must guard our minds against arrogance and evil thoughts.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_271.context: The king became proud due to his bad actions and evil thoughts, causing great conflict and trouble.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_273.meaning: We should avoid harsh judgment of others and instead seek understanding, allowing space for forgiveness and clarity.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_273.context: The speaker asks if his actions were right or wrong and urges listeners not to judge harshly in their hearts.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_608.meaning: Trustworthy friends help you handle hard tasks so you can focus on your own important path.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_608.context: Yudhisthira asks two strong leaders to guard the city while he leaves for a journey.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_609.meaning: Moving forward on your spiritual journey often requires crossing difficult or sacred boundaries with faith.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_609.context: King Yudhisthira travels to the battlefield area and crosses the holy river Yamuna with his group.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_610.meaning: We often see the results of our past actions before we fully understand their deep impact.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_610.context: Yudhisthira sees the forest home of his father Dhritarashtra from far away while walking through the land.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_611.meaning: Joy and community spirit can make even a wild place feel welcoming and full of life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_611.context: The happy crowd enters the forest area with great noise and excitement, following the king's lead.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_612.meaning: True strength is shown by being humble and respectful when you meet those who are older or wiser.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_612.context: The five Pandava brothers walk on foot to show respect and humility as they approach the hermitage.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_613.meaning: Leadership is about guiding others gently, and true loyalty means following your leader with a willing heart.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_613.context: All the citizens and country people follow the king, and the chief of the Kurus walks behind him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_614.meaning: Nature can be a peaceful place for reflection, reminding us that life continues even when people are gone.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_614.context: The Pandavas arrive at the empty hermitage, which is full of deer and decorated with banana trees.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_615.meaning: Curiosity and openness help us learn from wise people and discover new truths in unexpected places.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_615.context: Many holy men gather at the hermitage, and the Pandavas arrive there feeling very curious about what they will find.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1.meaning: Respectful prayer shows devotion and humility, reminding us to honor those we admire.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1.context: Abaravin Maya bows to Vasudeva, speaking kindly, in the Mahabharata story.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2.meaning: When we feel lost, asking for help shows trust and opens the way to safety.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2.context: A character asks for help, feeling angry and in danger, seeking guidance from Kaunteya.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_3.meaning: Gratitude builds good relationships and encourages others to keep helping us.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_3.context: Someone thanks a powerful demon and hopes for continued friendship and safety.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_4.meaning: Admiration inspires action, showing that we should act kindly before opportunities pass.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_4.context: A speaker praises a lord, wanting to act before a fairy, in a strange setting.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_5.meaning: Even enemies can help, teaching us to look beyond differences for common good.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_5.context: Visvakarma, a great demon poet, offers help to a Pandava in the epic.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_6.meaning: True freedom means we can still support others, even when we feel helpless.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_6.context: A person feels free from life’s troubles but cannot help others in their situation.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_7.meaning: Doing good work for others brings rewards and keeps our efforts meaningful.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_7.context: A demon urges action for Krishna, hoping for reward and not wanting effort wasted.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_8.meaning: Seeking wise counsel helps us understand people and make better choices.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_8.context: They urge a king to meet Krishna, questioning a woman’s nature in a moral debate.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_264.meaning: The verse shows how art and joy can bring happiness and unity among people.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_264.context: A king watches divine dancers and musicians, enjoying music, comedy, and joyful performances.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_266.meaning: It teaches that courage and strength can overcome even the most difficult challenges.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_266.context: A hero defeats powerful enemies named Bala and Vritra with great skill and bravery.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_267.meaning: The verse reminds us that wisdom and learning can illuminate our lives like bright light.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_267.context: Brahma and many sages fly in bright chariots, shining like fire across the sky.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_268.meaning: It shows that different people have different roles, and respect is given to those who guide others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_268.context: Some people travel while others wear garlands; wise men like Brihaspati and Venus appear.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_269.meaning: The verse highlights that many brave people work together to protect and support their community.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_269.context: A list of heroic names includes Rushad, Ashvo, Vasu, and others who are brave warriors.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_285.meaning: It teaches that teamwork and friendship help overcome difficult tasks and protect loved ones.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_285.context: Heroes like Kapot, Roma, Trinaka, Sahadeva, and Arjuna join Rama and Lakshmana in battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_286.meaning: The verse shows that loyalty and courage are essential to defend justice and protect others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_286.context: The same heroes join Rama, the king, and Lakshmana, the strong defender, in fighting enemies.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_287.meaning: It reminds us that many brave people can unite to achieve great goals and keep peace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_287.context: Warriors Alark, Kakshasena, Gayo, and Gaurashwa, along with Jamadagni, Rama, Nabhaga, and Sagara, appear.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_356.meaning: Witnessing divine or grand events can be overwhelming for ordinary people. Rest is needed after seeing such powerful sights.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_356.context: A speaker tells the king he saw a huge group in the sky and feels very tired now.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_357.meaning: The world changes over time. What seems permanent today may have been different in the distant past.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_357.context: The speaker recalls a time when the sun was not the ruler of the sky in ancient days.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_358.meaning: Stay authentic even when facing divine beings. Do not let outside appearances confuse your inner truth.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_358.context: The speaker advises the king to stay true to himself when seeing the assembly in human form.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_359.meaning: True power is used to bring happiness to others. Great beings shine with kindness and care for all.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_359.context: The speaker describes a being with great light who brings joy to all creatures through divine power.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_360.meaning: Some truths are hidden from us. We must seek guidance to understand what lies beyond our normal view.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_360.context: The speaker asks the lord how to see the grandfather assembly that is hidden by strict practices.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_362.meaning: We often look for easy tools to solve big problems. But some things require more than just tricks.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_362.context: The speaker asks if magic or medicine can help him see the assembly, seeking a practical way.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_363.meaning: You cannot trap or limit the divine. It is free and changes quickly beyond our control.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_363.context: The speaker notes that the being cannot be controlled or fixed in one shape because it changes fast.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_365.meaning: Accept that some things are beyond your knowledge. Humility helps when facing mysteries you cannot fully understand.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_365.context: The speaker admits he does not know the size or rules of this being and has never seen it.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_409.meaning: Powerful actions can bring victory, but true strength comes from wise leadership.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_409.context: Jaitra rides a gold chariot, conquering seven islands with powerful weapons.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_411.meaning: Great leaders honor traditions, showing respect for people and the divine.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_411.context: He rules all earth, known as mountain forest, and performs a great royal sacrifice.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_412.meaning: Sharing wealth honors the gods and builds unity among people.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_412.context: All earth rulers give wealth to him, acting as servants of the gods during sacrifice.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_413.meaning: Respecting spiritual guides strengthens a ruler’s moral authority.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_413.context: The king surrounds priests, giving them gifts, saying they are many times greater.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_414.meaning: Generosity attracts support and shows a ruler’s fairness.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_414.context: He gives wealth to Brahmins, and many creatures gather from all directions.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_415.meaning: True greatness shines when one serves others with generosity.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_415.context: He offers food, drink, gems, praised by gods, becoming fearless and bright.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_416.meaning: Great deeds make a king remembered and respected by all.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_416.context: Partha is told that Harish Chandra shines among thousands of kings.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_417.meaning: True leadership requires humility and a sincere heart.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_417.context: Harish Chandra completes sacrifice, repents, and shines when crowned with empire.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1112.meaning: True beauty comes from careful care and attention to detail in your daily life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1112.context: The text describes how the royal palace was beautifully decorated with gold and beads.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1113.meaning: A kind and pure heart makes a person naturally attractive and pleasant to others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1113.context: The people in the story wore flower garlands and had a very pleasant smell.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1114.meaning: Different people have different strengths, and we should respect all their unique talents.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1114.context: The scene compares the varied and high qualities of the people to mountain peaks.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1116.meaning: When good people come together, fairness and truth become clear and visible to all.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1116.context: Kings and wise teachers gathered together, and the light shone evenly on everyone.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1117.meaning: Showing respect to elders and teachers is a sign of a truly good character.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1117.context: Yudhisthira returned home and respectfully greeted his father, teachers, and other elders.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1118.meaning: Leaders should guide their family or team with clear and fair instructions.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1118.context: The eldest brother spoke to his siblings and started them on the right path.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1120.meaning: Clear rules help prevent confusion and keep social events running smoothly and fairly.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1120.context: The text mentions confusion about rules for food and drink during a marriage event.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1121.meaning: We should always recognize and appreciate the good work that others do for us.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1121.context: Sanjaya was asked to honor the kings and wise teachers for their good deeds.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1297.meaning: When you face cruel words, your inner strength can rise up to protect your dignity.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1297.context: Bhima heard harsh insults and his powerful body reacted with intense strength and rage.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1298.meaning: Even calm people can feel sudden anger, and their faces may show that hidden fire.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1298.context: Bhima looked beautiful like a lotus, but his eyes turned red with deep anger.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1299.meaning: A strong person's face can look like a storm, showing the power inside them.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1299.context: Kings saw Bhima's forehead look like a sea crest or a river path.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1300.meaning: Extreme anger can feel like a destructive force that consumes everything around you.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1300.context: Bhima gritted his teeth and looked angry, like the world burning at the end of time.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1301.meaning: Wise leaders can stop fights by speaking gently and helping angry people find peace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1301.context: Bhishma stopped Bhima from fighting and used kind words to calm his anger.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1303.meaning: True strength means staying steady and brave when someone tries to make you angry.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1303.context: Shishupala made Bhima angry, but Bhima stood firm and did not shake or fear.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1304.meaning: Confidence helps you act fast, but seeing others as weak can lead to bad choices.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1304.context: Bhima jumped up quickly to fight, seeing his enemy as small as a deer.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1306.meaning: Sometimes people mock others who are angry, not realizing the real power behind the emotion.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1306.context: The angry king laughed at Bhima, seeing him as very strong and full of rage.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1525.meaning: Ignoring good advice leads to bad outcomes. You must listen to truth to avoid serious trouble and keep yourself safe from harm.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1525.context: A speaker warns the king that he will face certain death if he ignores wise counsel and continues his current path.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1526.meaning: Do not worry about losing power. True happiness comes from accepting your fate and letting go of control over others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1526.context: Vidura tells the king he will rule the earth after death, questioning why the king cares so much about him now.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1527.meaning: Bad company can cloud your judgment. Listen to those who care for your soul, not just those who agree with your mistakes.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1527.context: Dhritarashtra hears his mother speak in distress while standing with Duryodhana, who supports the wrong side of the argument.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1528.meaning: Pride in wealth can blind us. Focusing on outward beauty often hides inner problems and leads to dangerous traps for others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1528.context: The king orders craftsmen to make a large hall with many doors look beautiful and spectacular for an upcoming event.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1529.meaning: True value is not in jewels. Focus on doing good actions and understanding right behavior rather than showing off rich possessions.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1529.context: Someone is covered in gems and asked to slowly explain good deeds and the proper way to enter a place.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1530.meaning: Choosing family loyalty over truth is wrong. You must stand for what is right, even if it hurts your loved ones.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1530.context: The king decides that peace with Duryodhana is best, effectively ignoring the wise advice given by his brother Vidura.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1531.meaning: Love should not blind you to truth. You must see people as they are, not just how you wish them to be.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1531.context: The king ignores Vidura because he is too attached to his sons, failing to see their faults clearly.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1532.meaning: Wisdom often arrives when we are lost. Seek guidance when you feel defeated, as truth can help you rise again.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1532.context: Vidura appears at the gate after hearing news, while Dhritarashtra rises from a state of deep despair and confusion.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1993.meaning: Public opinion can rise quickly to support justice and shame those who act with cruelty and disrespect.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1993.context: The crowd shouts loudly to praise Vikarna and condemn Saubala for their actions in the court.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1994.meaning: Extreme anger can cloud your judgment and lead to impulsive actions that hurt yourself and others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1994.context: Radha faints from anger at the noise and grabs someone to speak harsh words to them.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1995.meaning: Lies and false actions spread quickly and cause total destruction to the moral fabric of society.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1995.context: Many distortions of truth are visible here, acting like a forest fire that destroys everything in its path.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1996.meaning: Oppressors often twist the truth to justify their cruelty, claiming victory even when they are clearly wrong.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1996.context: Even when choked by Krishna, the speaker claims righteousness has conquered the daughter of Drupada in the game.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1997.meaning: Blind love for family can destroy your wisdom and prevent you from seeing the truth clearly.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1997.context: Dhritarashtra is torn apart by his childish attachment to his sons and what he said in the assembly.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1998.meaning: Ignorance of moral law makes people confused and unable to accept reality, leading to foolish arguments.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1998.context: Duryodhana does not know the truth of dharma and is slow-witted, claiming Krishna is both conquered and unconquered.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1999.meaning: When justice is ignored, the innocent suffer, and the powerful try to hide their failure to protect them.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1999.context: Draupadi stands inside the assembly, and the speaker questions why Krishna is said to have conquered dharma but not her.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2000.meaning: True righteousness cannot be defeated by force, even when the innocent appear to be humiliated by evil.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2000.context: Draupadi remains present in the assembly, and the speaker asks why righteousness is said to be conquered but not her.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2001.meaning: Pride leads to downfall. Do not believe you are above justice or immune to the consequences of your cruel actions.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2001.context: Draupadi questions the Kauravas about their arrogance and false sense of power during the unfair dice game.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2002.meaning: Public shame exposes evil. When people see wrongdoing clearly, they cannot ignore the moral failure of the leaders.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2002.context: Draupadi challenges the assembly to witness the injustice done to her in front of all the elders present.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2003.meaning: Sacred bonds protect us. Respect the commitments made under divine guidance, as they carry spiritual weight and duty.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2003.context: Draupadi reminds the court that she was married to five husbands according to divine will and law.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2004.meaning: Dignity matters always. Treating someone with disrespect in public shows a deep lack of character and moral courage.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2004.context: Draupadi questions why the elders allow her to be brought into the hall in such a humiliating state.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2005.meaning: Fairness is key. If you earn something honestly, you deserve respect for it, not humiliation or loss of rights.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2005.context: Draupadi argues that the Pandavas won their wealth fairly, so she should not be treated as a slave.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2006.meaning: Silence can be complicity. Failing to protect those you love when they are in danger is a moral failure.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2006.context: The Pandavas sit silently in the assembly while their wife is being disrespected and stripped of her dignity.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2008.meaning: Cruelty has limits. Violating someone's bodily autonomy in public is a grave sin that invites divine and social judgment.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2008.context: Dushasana drags Draupadi by her hair and tries to strip her clothes in the middle of the royal court.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2009.meaning: Divine protection exists. When you are innocent and wronged, higher powers often intervene to preserve your dignity and honor.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2009.context: As Dushasana pulls her sari, it becomes endless, protecting Draupadi from being exposed before the assembly.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2048.meaning: Seeking the highest truth helps us understand our purpose and guides us toward living a righteous and meaningful life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2048.context: The crowd listens to Krishna ask a deep question about the highest truth and duty in life.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2049.meaning: Using cruel words to hurt others shows a lack of respect and reveals the speaker's own inner darkness.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2049.context: Karna insults the Pandavas by calling them servants while the kings remain silent during the tense gambling match.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2050.meaning: Publicly shaming a vulnerable person is a grave injustice that destroys dignity and violates the sacred laws of honor.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2050.context: Duryodhana drags the frightened Draupadi into the public assembly to humiliate her after winning her in the dice game.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2051.meaning: Silence in the face of evil makes us complicit, so we must speak up when we see wrongs being committed.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2051.context: A speaker addresses the teachers in the court, claiming they are not responsible for the terrible events happening now.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2053.meaning: Physical violence against the helpless causes immense suffering and highlights the complete breakdown of moral order and justice.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2053.context: Draupadi is grabbed and lifted up by her hair, causing her to fall and cry out in deep pain.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2054.meaning: When a woman is dishonored in public, it shows that the society has lost its protective values and moral compass.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2054.context: Draupadi laments that she, who was once protected in her home, now stands exposed and dishonored in the court.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2056.meaning: The fall from high honor to public shame shows how quickly values can collapse when power is abused without restraint.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2056.context: She notes that her family once feared even the wind touching her, but now they endure this cruel treatment.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2057.meaning: When leaders allow cruelty and injustice to flourish, it signals the decline of society and the loss of divine order.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2057.context: She believes this terrible treatment marks the end of time because the Kurus allow such unworthy acts to happen.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_34.meaning: We should care for others, even when it is difficult, because it helps everyone feel safer.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_34.context: People work hard to protect others, feeling sad and worried for everyone.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_35.meaning: Treat everyone kindly, even those who make mistakes, to avoid harsh judgment and build compassion.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_35.context: Some people turned away and were punished, while the speaker urges love for all.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_36.meaning: Doing good deeds brings inner peace and honor, showing that true strength comes from kindness.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_36.context: The speaker talks about their heart’s awareness and feeling proud of good actions.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_37.meaning: Open hearts to strangers, and listen to their pain, because compassion creates safety for all.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_37.context: A righteous king welcomed foreigners, but they cried in distress, calling for help.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_38.meaning: Honoring good qualities keeps people united; ignoring them leads to sadness and division.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_38.context: Remembering a hero’s virtues, people felt sorrow and turned away, causing distress for the Pandavas.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_39.meaning: Traveling together in nature reminds us that teamwork and calm help us reach new places.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_39.context: After night, the Pandavas rode chariots into a forest by the river Jahnavi.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_40.meaning: Taking time to refresh and rest strengthens us for future challenges and keeps our spirits bright.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_40.context: The Pandavas rested near a banyan tree, bathing in clean water after a tiring day.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_41.meaning: Sharing stories and learning from each other around a fire builds wisdom and community.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_41.context: Fires were lit by others, and a wise conversation happened among the Brahmaghosha.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_227.meaning: True leaders admit their mistakes and ask for forgiveness to heal broken relationships and show humility.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_227.context: The king feels deep shame after yelling at his wise minister and wants to make amends.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_228.meaning: Forgiveness is powerful when we respect the person we hurt and see their good intentions clearly.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_228.context: Vidura accepts the apology because he respects the king as a teacher and a guide for the people.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_229.meaning: Focus on the good people around you and do not let fear of poverty cloud your judgment.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_229.context: Vidura tells the king that good people exist and he should not worry about being poor.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_230.meaning: Even powerful people feel weak sometimes and need the love and support of their family.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_230.context: The king feels like a poor man and cries out to his daughters for comfort and support.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_231.meaning: Kind words between friends can bring joy and peace to everyone involved in the situation.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_231.context: Two bright brothers talk to each other and make both Vidura and the king feel very happy.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_232.meaning: People with bad intentions often feel upset when others choose peace and understanding instead of conflict.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_232.context: The wicked prince hears that the king has made peace with Vidura and feels very sad about it.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_233.meaning: Sometimes we need to gather close friends to talk through our darkest and most confusing thoughts.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_233.context: The king brings his advisors into a dark room to talk about his confused and troubled mind.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_234.meaning: A true friend is wise, loyal, and always works to help others live better and happier lives.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_234.context: The king notes that Vidura is a wise friend who always cares about the Pandava brothers.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_324.meaning: We pray for peace and ask wise help to avoid harm and keep everyone safe.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_324.context: King Dhritarashtra asks a sage to stop a bad event from happening.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_325.meaning: Good actions bring calm; bad actions bring trouble, so choose kindness and honesty.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_325.context: A king is told his son will be peaceful if he follows good ways.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_326.meaning: Unexpected victories show that courage and skill can overcome strong enemies.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_326.context: Duryodhana’s father is shocked when Maitreya talks about Bhima beating Kirmir.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_327.meaning: Honesty matters; we should speak truth even when it is hard to keep promises.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_327.context: A man says he will not lie about his son, and promises to reveal truth later.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_328.meaning: Fear of loss reminds us to protect loved ones and act with care.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_328.context: Maitreya stands up, and Duryodhana worries about Kirmir’s death.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_329.meaning: Knowing how to fight well helps us defend ourselves and others from danger.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_329.context: Someone wants to shoot Kirmir with a sword and asks how Bhima fought him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_330.meaning: Remembering heroic deeds inspires us to be brave and strong in our own lives.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_330.context: A story about Bhima’s great strength is told again at the end of the tales.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_331.meaning: After defeat, we must keep moving forward, find new places, and stay hopeful.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_331.context: The Pandavas leave after losing to Dayuta and travel to the forest Kamyaka.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_507.meaning: When we face hardships, we should seek simple, humble living and trust in divine help.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_507.context: People suffer many troubles, feeling very distressed, asking Krishna to live without nobility.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_508.meaning: Even powerful allies may not help; we must rely on inner strength and faith.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_508.context: Strong lions are powerful, yet the speaker feels ignored during suffering.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_509.meaning: True compassion involves enduring pain for others, learning to forgive and move forward.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_509.context: Weak people endure suffering, burning for others' sins and bad deeds.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_510.meaning: Her noble birth reminds us that family ties can bring honor and responsibility.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_510.context: Born into a great family, she is the beloved wife of the Pandavas and daughter-in-law.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_511.meaning: In sorrow, we can find calm by speaking gently and seeking inner light.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_511.context: Krishna covers her face, cries, and speaks softly with lotus hair and light.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_513.meaning: Anger mixed with tears shows deep pain; we should express feelings honestly.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_513.context: She wipes her eyes, sighs, and speaks angrily with tears in her throat.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_515.meaning: Loneliness can be profound, but we can find support in community and faith.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_515.context: She says she has no husband, son, brother, father, or relatives.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_516.meaning: Neglect hurts deeply; we should listen and care for those in pain.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_516.context: Those who neglect her cause grief; her sorrow cannot be eased by laughter.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_698.meaning: True strength comes from inner power, not just weapons. You cannot be defeated if your spirit is unbreakable.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_698.context: A warrior tells his enemy that a special arrow makes him impossible to kill in battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_699.meaning: Fate controls life and death. Sometimes, higher powers step in to protect those who are meant to survive.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_699.context: Death is described as a powerful force that gods enjoy, but divine will protects the innocent from harm.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_700.meaning: When danger comes, act with calm confidence. Being prepared and ready helps you face challenges without fear.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_700.context: Paradyumna feels happy and ready for the fight. He quickly grabs his bow to defend himself.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_701.meaning: Sometimes, running away is the smart choice. Knowing when to retreat can save your life and strength.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_701.context: Shalva is angry and hurt by arrows. He runs away from the battlefield to find safety elsewhere.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_702.meaning: Bad actions lead to suffering. Even powerful people must face the consequences of their cruelty and choices.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_702.context: A cruel king leaves his city after being tormented by enemies. He eventually dies and goes to heaven.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_703.meaning: Duty and service are important. Completing hard tasks with dedication brings honor and peace to your community.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_703.context: A hero reports that he freed a city and completed a major religious sacrifice for the king.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_704.meaning: Things change over time. What was once beautiful can be ruined, reminding us that nothing lasts forever.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_704.context: A traveler sees a beautiful city that has been destroyed. The people there look sad and unadorned.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_705.meaning: Trust your instincts when things feel wrong. Asking for help from someone you trust is a wise move.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_705.context: The traveler sees strange, unrecognizable places and feels suspicious. He asks a close person for help.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_778.meaning: True strength comes from protecting the good and removing evil from the world around us.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_778.context: A warrior speaks to Bharata about his victory over many evil demons in battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_779.meaning: Seeking wise guidance can fill your heart with positive feelings and clear your mind.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_779.context: The hero visits a wise teacher and feels a deep sense of hope and joy.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_780.meaning: Sometimes bad forces create sudden chaos that feels overwhelming and hard to control.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_780.context: A demon turns into a monkey and causes chaos by making rocks fall from the sky.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_781.meaning: When life feels too heavy, remember that even small things can survive great pressure.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_781.context: The speaker feels crushed by falling rocks and compares himself to a tiny ant.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_782.meaning: In hard times, choosing a safe place to rest can help you recover your strength.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_782.context: The hero picks a specific mountain to hide in while his driver follows him closely.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_783.meaning: Even wise people can feel scared when danger comes fast, and running is sometimes okay.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_783.context: The enemy attacks, and the wise teachers run away in fear from the sudden danger.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_784.meaning: When you feel lost, it is normal to feel like the world has turned against you.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_784.context: The speaker laments that the gods and the world seem to have disappeared into darkness.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_785.meaning: It is healthy to show your sadness and let your friends see your true feelings.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_785.context: The hero's friends are very sad and cry loudly because of the terrible events happening.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_768.meaning: Seeing your own people hurt makes you feel deep pain and worry for them.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_768.context: Rama fights hard with spears while his own brave warriors fall in the battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_769.meaning: Love for family can make you forget the fight and see what truly matters.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_769.context: The hero wakes up from a trance and sees his father instead of enemies.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_770.meaning: Staying calm helps you see the truth and act with focus and power.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_770.context: The warrior calms his mind, sees the enemy clearly, and shoots many arrows.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_771.meaning: You can protect yourself and others by choosing the right tools and staying strong.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_771.context: The hero picks up a new bow and stops the enemy arrows and swords.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_773.meaning: Even when things look scary, your inner peace can keep you safe and steady.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_773.context: Scary demons with wild hair appear, but the king feels safe inside his mind.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_774.meaning: Your inner strength matters more than the frightening things you see around you.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_774.context: The group of ugly demons shows up, but the king remains calm within himself.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_775.meaning: When trouble makes a loud noise, you must stay ready to handle it wisely.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_775.context: A loud sound like a battle starts, and the hero plans to stop it.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_776.meaning: Life has many confusing sounds, so you must listen carefully to find the truth.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_776.context: Another strange sound comes from above, and the king hears a different voice.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_990.meaning: Keeping your cool during hard times brings true happiness. Anger only hurts you. Peace leads to a better life for everyone.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_990.context: Wise people stay calm when things go wrong. They do not get mad at trouble. They find peace later.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_991.meaning: Forgiveness is a brave choice for everyone. It shows great strength. Letting go of hate makes you a better person always.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_991.context: You should forgive people whether they are strong or weak. Forgive them even if it seems risky or dangerous to you.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_992.meaning: Winning by being kind is better than fighting. Righteousness comes from mercy. True success is found in forgiving others completely.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_992.context: Holy people praise winning through forgiveness. This kind of victory is seen as the most right and good action.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_993.meaning: Honesty beats lying every single time. Anger hides your faults. Do not let anger drive you to hurt others or yourself.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_993.context: Truth is better than lies. Anger causes many faults. Why create more trouble by killing someone in a fit of rage?

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_994.meaning: Be like the wise judge who stays calm. Fear and anger cloud your mind. Stay clear and brave to see the truth.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_994.context: Wise people say the god of justice is bright. He does not feel fear or anger. He stays calm and clear.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_995.meaning: Controlling your temper when provoked shows true wisdom. It proves you are strong. Master your emotions to be seen as great.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_995.context: If you stop your anger when others provoke you, wise people call you brilliant. You control your own mind well.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_996.meaning: Anger blinds you to reality and rules. You lose your way. Stay calm so you can see what is right and fair.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_996.context: An angry person cannot see others clearly. They lose their sense of duty and boundaries. They act without thinking or care.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_997.meaning: Anger destroys your spiritual growth and respect. You must remove it. Only then can you do your duty with a pure heart.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_997.context: Even if you meditate, anger ruins your progress. Beating a teacher is wrong. Remove anger to follow your true duty well.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_980.meaning: Understanding anger's impact, one can control it. Forgiveness and kindness bring peace, not anger.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_980.context: In Hinduism, Lord Krishna advises Arjuna about the consequences of anger. Book 3, Chapter 980 of the Mahabharata.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_981.meaning: Anger stems from seeing others as a threat. Wise people overcome anger by understanding others' perspectives.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_981.context: Mahabharata Book 3, Chapter 981. Lord Krishna explains the root of anger.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_982.meaning: Anger harms oneself and others. Patience and understanding bring harmony.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_982.context: Mahabharata Book 3, Chapter 984. Lord Krishna talks about anger's destructive nature.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_983.meaning: Control your thoughts and actions to avoid negative consequences.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_983.context: Mahabharata Book 3, Chapter 985. Lord Krishna discusses the importance of self-control.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_986.meaning: Anger leads to destruction. Control it for personal and societal well-being.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_986.context: Mahabharata Book 3, Chapter 986. Lord Krishna teaches about anger's destructive nature.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_987.meaning: Selflessness brings strength and peace. Understand others' perspectives to overcome anger.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_987.context: Mahabharata Book 3, Chapter 987. Lord Krishna explains the power of selflessness.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_988.meaning: Anger harms oneself and others. Patience and understanding bring harmony.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_988.context: Mahabharata Book 3, Chapter 988. Lord Krishna talks about the consequences of anger.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_989.meaning: Control your thoughts and actions for personal and societal well-being.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_989.context: Mahabharata Book 3, Chapter 989. Lord Krishna discusses the importance of self-control.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1653.meaning: Stay calm when trouble comes because truth protects you. Do not worry about the future or fear what is coming.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1653.context: A wise speaker describes a truthful person who will face danger soon without fear or anxiety.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1654.meaning: Seek to be known for good deeds. Stand with your family and friends to show strength and unity to all.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1654.context: A king speaks to a divine figure, asking to be seen by everyone alongside his brothers in unity.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1655.meaning: Cleanse your mind and actions to find peace. A clear conscience brings true happiness and freedom from worry.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1655.context: A ruler is told that cleansing rituals remove sin and fever, leading to a happy and peaceful kingdom.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1658.meaning: Watch for hidden dangers in rough places. Protect your community from evil forces that seek to harm the innocent.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1658.context: Demons live in dangerous mountain forts. The speaker advises the king to protect his people from these threats.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1660.meaning: Great actions inspire wonder in others. Listen to how wise leaders react to news of courage and heroic deeds.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1660.context: The narrator praises Arjuna's amazing deeds and asks what the blind king Dhritarashtra said upon hearing the news.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1663.meaning: News of great journeys spreads quickly. Share important updates with trusted friends so everyone knows the truth.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1663.context: Indra learns that Arjuna has traveled to a new world. A sage speaks to Sanjaya about this event.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1664.meaning: Seek truth from reliable sources. Ask those who know the facts to confirm what you have heard about others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1664.context: A king tells his charioteer that he has heard all about Arjuna's wise deeds and asks for confirmation.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1665.meaning: Pride and bad choices lead to ruin. Recognize when anger or ego is driving someone toward harmful actions.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1665.context: A father warns that his wicked son is drunk on power and will bring destruction to the earth.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3685.meaning: When order breaks down, sacred duties are neglected. This shows how chaos disrupts the harmony and peace of daily life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3685.context: The earth suffered great chaos as sacred fires were scattered and broken by natural forces during a time of turmoil.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3686.meaning: Fear can stop us from doing good deeds. We must keep our faith even when the world seems dark and hopeless.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3686.context: People stopped their religious studies and rituals because the world felt dark, scary, and full of deep discouragement and fear.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3687.meaning: Panic leads to destruction. We should face our fears with courage instead of running away from our problems.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3687.context: Humans were destroyed by panic because they were too afraid to protect themselves and ran away in sheer terror.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3688.meaning: Despair can make us give up. We must find hope and strength to survive difficult times instead of quitting.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3688.context: People hid in caves or streams, while others gave up their lives because they were too anxious and scared.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3689.meaning: Courage and effort are needed to fight evil. We must stand up against wrongdoers with bravery and determination.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3689.context: Brave and proud archers tried very hard to find and fight the demons that were causing trouble for everyone.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3690.meaning: Pride can lead to failure. We must be humble and wise when facing challenges that seem impossible to overcome.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3690.context: The warriors failed to defeat the demons hiding in the sea and suffered shame and decay for their defeat.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3691.meaning: Remembering past struggles helps us understand current problems. We learn from history to handle future crises better.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3691.context: The speaker reminds the king about past sacrifices and how the sea caused great distress and trouble for the world.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3693.meaning: Divine help comes in unexpected forms. We should trust that support will arrive to save us from disaster.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3693.context: The divine being took the form of a boar to lift the earth from the sea and save the universe.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3772.meaning: The king celebrates his many warriors, showing pride in his lineage and the strength of his family.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3772.context: A king speaks of sixty thousand brave sons, proud of war, born from his wives.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3773.meaning: He feels joy and gratitude for his family, recognizing the blessings of his household.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3773.context: King Sagara visits all his homes, pleased with his wives and their children.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3775.meaning: Their pregnancies promise new life and continuity for the king's lineage.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3775.context: The king's wife Vaidarbhi and Saibya become pregnant, bringing hope for future heirs.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3776.meaning: The births strengthen the family, showing the blessings of fertility and divine favor.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3776.context: Vaidarbhi gives birth to a son, and Saibya also has a child, both in good health.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3777.meaning: He listens to nature’s call, showing respect for the environment and its guidance.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3777.context: The king decides to release water, hearing a deep voice from the earth.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3778.meaning: He is advised to protect his children and preserve their future through careful planning.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3778.context: The king is told not to abandon his sons, to hide seeds carefully in alabaster.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3779.meaning: The offering symbolizes generosity, leading to blessings of many descendants and prosperity.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3779.context: Vessels filled with butter are offered, promising sixty thousand sons for the king.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3780.meaning: He is reminded to act wisely, trusting divine purpose and living a righteous life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_3780.context: The king learns his son’s birth was destined by Mahadeva, urging him to follow karma-yoga.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4211.meaning: Dedication and quiet focus help us grow stronger in spirit and find inner peace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4211.context: Chayavana is a holy man who meditates quietly by a lake to gain spiritual power.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4212.meaning: Staying committed to your goals over time brings great rewards and personal growth.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4212.context: The bright sage Chayavana continues his strict spiritual practices near the water for many years.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4213.meaning: Patience and staying still in your purpose show true strength and deep devotion.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4213.context: He remained in one spot for a very long time without moving or changing position.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4214.meaning: True dedication means ignoring outside appearances and focusing only on your inner spiritual journey.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4214.context: Nature covered him with dirt and ants so he looked like a lifeless statue.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4216.meaning: Time moves forward constantly while spiritual truths remain steady and unchanged for all people.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4216.context: Years passed and a new king named Sharyatira ruled the land near that sacred lake.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4217.meaning: We are born into different circumstances but our choices define who we truly become.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4217.context: The king had many wives and one beautiful daughter named Shubhra who lived in the palace.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4218.meaning: Curiosity and kindness can lead us to discover hidden wisdom in unexpected places.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4218.context: The princess walked with her friends near the lake and found the sage covered in ants.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4219.meaning: Finding joy in simple nature and holy company brings happiness to the heart.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4219.context: She was happy to see the sage and enjoyed looking for plants with her friends nearby.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4610.meaning: Show kindness and support to friends, and honor the respect of family and elders.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4610.context: A warrior comforts a friend, promising help, while his father respects him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4611.meaning: Speak truthfully to loved ones, even if it does not please everyone around you.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4611.context: He speaks boldly to his father, not pleasing the wise teachers with grand speeches.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4612.meaning: Confidence and calmness help you reach important places and people in life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4612.context: He walks confidently to his father's hermitage during the month of Madhava.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4613.meaning: Beauty and calm surroundings can inspire peace and reflection in everyday life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4613.context: He sees a beautiful hermitage with flowering trees and a wandering daughter-in-law.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4614.meaning: Encourage people to act bravely and be aware of their own motives.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4614.context: Yavacris urges her to stand up, calling her shameless and unaware of desire.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4615.meaning: Helping those who feel alone brings them closer to supportive communities.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4615.context: He lifts the lonely spirit, arriving at Raibhya's ashram, named Arindam.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4616.meaning: Repeated acts of kindness strengthen bonds and create lasting support.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4616.context: He lifts the lonely spirit again, reaching Raibhya's ashram, Arindam.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4617.meaning: Comforting others with gentle words helps heal pain and builds trust.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4617.context: Seeing his daughter-in-law cry, Paravasos comforts her, and Yudhisthira speaks gently.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4899.meaning: Even powerful beings can be tired; rest is important for everyone, no matter how strong.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4899.context: A big monkey named Hanuman yawned, causing the chief of monkeys to fall asleep.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4900.meaning: Show your strength and courage, even when you feel sleepy or weak.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4900.context: Hanuman yawned again, raising a huge flag like a banner while sleeping among banana trees.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4901.meaning: A loud voice can spread far, reminding us that our actions can influence many.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4901.context: In a mountain cave, a roar echoed from a tail, sounding like a white shout.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4902.meaning: Noise can come from unexpected places, teaching us to listen carefully to find truth.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4902.context: The sound of a tail echoed like a drunken elephant, hidden on mountain slopes.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4903.meaning: Curiosity drives us to discover new things, and listening helps us learn more.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4903.context: Bhima heard a thrilling sound and searched for its source in the banana forest.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4904.meaning: Powerful leaders stand firm, showing that confidence comes from a strong foundation.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4904.context: In the forest, a rock held the mighty monkey lord standing proudly.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4905.meaning: Even small creatures can inspire, reminding us that beauty and courage come in many forms.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4905.context: A chick with a broken head and long hair shone like a flag, moving upward.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4908.meaning: Appearance can reflect inner joy, encouraging us to share happiness with others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4908.context: Lad Bharuvam had red lips, a copper tongue, and red ears, with a bright smile.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5025.meaning: Showing sincere devotion in your daily duties and rituals helps you connect with the divine and maintain spiritual balance in life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5025.context: The speaker urges the Bharata king to perform sacred rituals and offer gifts to the gods with deep devotion and respect.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5026.meaning: Living a life of integrity and understanding true moral laws brings peace and respect from others in your community.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5026.context: A son advises his father to follow his duties strictly and understand the highest form of righteousness and moral conduct.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5027.meaning: True moral law is clear to the wise, while confusion arises when people focus on petty divisions instead of universal truth.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5027.context: The text explains that foolish people are confused by divisions, but even gods like Jupiter understand the true nature of duty.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5030.meaning: Following ancient spiritual laws and rituals keeps the cosmic order balanced and helps humans live in harmony with nature.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5030.context: Gods are sustained by Vedic sacrifices and rituals, while humans uphold these laws through the guidance of wise teachers.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5031.meaning: Honest work in farming and trade is a sacred duty that supports society and connects us to the divine order.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5031.context: Trade, agriculture, and animal husbandry are described as the main ways that heavenly races and humans sustain their livelihoods.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5032.meaning: Fair laws and just leadership are essential for guiding society safely through life and maintaining peace among all people.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5032.context: The third science of statecraft and punishment is discussed, showing how proper governance guides the journey of the world.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5033.meaning: Justice requires both moral behavior and fair consequences, otherwise society falls into disorder and people suffer greatly.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5033.context: Without righteous action and proper punishment, there is no true justice on earth, and chaos would spread without limits.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5034.meaning: Some spiritual practices are more powerful than others, so focus on the most significant acts to gain the greatest blessings.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5034.context: The horse sacrifice is called the best nectar of righteousness, while other rituals like study and gifts are considered ordinary.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5194.meaning: Anger can make people rush into conflict without thinking about the bad results that follow.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5194.context: Two brothers from the Madri family got very angry and ran at each other to fight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5195.meaning: A strong person can calm a fight and show confidence in their own ability to solve problems.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5195.context: Vrikodara laughed at the fighting brothers and stopped them, saying he could handle the demon alone.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5196.meaning: When rivals meet, they often prepare for battle, showing that competition can quickly turn into serious conflict.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5196.context: Two powerful heroes started competing with each other, and both sides picked up their weapons to fight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5198.meaning: Great evil forces can seem overwhelming and terrifying, making the struggle against them feel very difficult.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5198.context: Angry and scary demons fought in a huge battle, with numbers so large it was hard to count.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5199.meaning: Violence can be loud and chaotic, like a storm, shaking the peace of the surrounding area.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5199.context: Fighters climbed trees and hit each other, sounding like loud thunder clouds at the end of summer.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5200.meaning: Deep rivalry can make people use all their strength, even against nature, to try and win.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5200.context: Two very strong men used their legs to push against huge trees while fighting each other fiercely.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5201.meaning: Family conflicts can cause widespread destruction, hurting the environment and everyone around the fighters.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5201.context: A war broke out that destroyed many trees, involving Vali, Sugriva, and their monkey brothers.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5202.meaning: Lack of wisdom leads to endless, noisy conflict where no one truly wins or finds peace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5202.context: Two forces of ignorance hit each other, and both sides kept screaming and beating each other repeatedly.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5357.meaning: True strength comes from seeing through fear and showing others that their worries are not real threats.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5357.context: A hero stands on a high peak to show others how fear is just an illusion.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5358.meaning: Facing difficult challenges requires courage, even when your opponent struggles to handle the pressure of the situation.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5358.context: A powerful warrior enters a dark cave while his rival watches with great difficulty and pain.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5360.meaning: When you stay united and confident with your family, you become strong and inspiring to everyone around you.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5360.context: The noble brothers stand together with pride and strength, shining like bright gold in the sun.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5361.meaning: Respect your tools and prepare yourself well, because readiness and dignity are signs of a true leader.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5361.context: A handsome warrior with long arms touches his bow, sword, and quiver with great care and respect.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5363.meaning: Great power can cause fear in others, so use your strength wisely and with compassion for all.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5363.context: The mountain shakes with fear, like an elephant separated from its herd, showing great power and awe.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5364.meaning: Even in tough times, stand firm and ready, because your courage inspires respect and fear in others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5364.context: A warrior looks fierce like a dying lion, holding weapons while all creatures watch him in awe.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5365.meaning: True peace arrives when you let go of jealousy and worry, allowing love and calm to fill your heart.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5365.context: A speaker asks when fear and envy disappear, suggesting a time of peace and pure love.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5367.meaning: Seeking truth often means facing scary heights, but climbing up gives you a clearer view of reality.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5367.context: A strong man climbs a very high and scary peak to see a strange and terrible sight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5346.meaning: Seeking wisdom from elders helps us grow in character and understand our path in life better.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5346.context: The wise brothers visited a holy man to seek guidance and share their spiritual journey together.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5348.meaning: Life brings sudden changes and losses that remind us to stay calm and accept what happens.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5348.context: A powerful bird stole a rich snake while the narrator lived near a large lake for days.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5349.meaning: Good deeds and pure thoughts spread like fragrance, bringing peace and joy to those around us.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5349.context: A gentle wind blew from a high mountain, carrying the sweet scent of holy flowers everywhere.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5351.meaning: Being with loved ones in a holy place strengthens bonds and brings deep spiritual happiness to all.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5351.context: The heroes saw divine flowers and their friends, including their wife, in a sacred and bright place.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5352.meaning: Quiet moments with a wise friend allow for deep conversations that guide us through hard times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5352.context: Krishna spoke to Bhima while they sat quietly on a lonely mountain side during their journey.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5353.meaning: Remembering past victories gives us confidence and strength to face new challenges with courage and faith.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5353.context: Krishna reminded Arjuna of how he defeated demons and recovered his famous bow in the past.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5355.meaning: Our unique talents and strengths are gifts that should be used wisely to help others and do good.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5355.context: Krishna praised Bhima for his incredible physical strength and radiant glory, comparing him to many sacrifices.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5356.meaning: When we use our power to protect the weak, evil forces retreat and peace is restored to the land.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5356.context: Bhima defeated many demons with his speed and strength, forcing them to flee in all directions.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5733.meaning: Big events can feel overwhelming and scary, but they are just part of the natural flow of life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5733.context: The battle scene is described as huge and loud, like big mountains moving in the ocean.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5734.meaning: When trouble comes fast, you must stay calm and ready to defend yourself with skill.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5734.context: A strong enemy attacks the hero quickly, shooting many sharp arrows at him from a distance.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5735.meaning: Conflict can be very destructive, so we should always seek peace before fighting begins.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5735.context: The speaker describes a loud and terrible blow that shook the air and the battlefield.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5736.meaning: When many people fight together, the situation becomes messy and hard for anyone to control.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5736.context: Many different groups of gods, sages, and demons join together in one massive and chaotic fight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5737.meaning: Flattery can be a trap, so you must listen carefully and not let nice words fool you.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5737.context: Enemies try to win the hero over using sweet words and praise, just like they praised Indra.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5738.meaning: People may use tools or power that do not belong to them, so trust their actions, not their words.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5738.context: A group of fast demons rushes at the hero, holding weapons that they took from others.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5739.meaning: You may feel trapped by enemies on all sides, but you must find a way to break free.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5739.context: Charioteers shout loudly and block the path, surrounding the hero and shooting arrows from all sides.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5740.meaning: New challenges will keep coming, so you must stay strong and keep moving forward.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5740.context: More strong warriors arrive with spears and lances, throwing them at the hero in the battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5767.meaning: Sometimes life hits us with sudden, overwhelming force that we cannot control or avoid.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5767.context: A warrior describes being hit by powerful divine weapons during a fierce and chaotic battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5768.meaning: Trouble often comes in unexpected forms, turning ordinary things into sources of danger.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5768.context: During the tenth year of conflict, a strange fire appears and stone dust falls like flames.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5769.meaning: When we feel surrounded by death, we must stay calm and focused on our path.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5769.context: Heavy rain falls in the tenth year, and the speaker feels trapped by deadly weapons.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5770.meaning: Challenges can come from all sides, so we must be ready to face any direction.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5770.context: Sharp streams of energy pour from the sky, covering every direction the warriors move.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5771.meaning: In times of chaos, we must trust our inner voice when the world is too loud.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5771.context: Streams fall and wind blows loudly, making it hard to hear or see clearly.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5772.meaning: Confusion can make us stumble, but we must keep trying to stand up again.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5772.context: Energy streams connect heaven and earth, confusing the speaker and causing them to fall.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5773.meaning: Powerful forces can change the environment, reminding us that nature is not always stable.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5773.context: A divine weapon named Vishosana is used, causing the water to dry up completely.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5774.meaning: Do not be fooled by scary illusions; focus on what is real and true in your life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5774.context: The speaker stops the rain, while demons release fake fire and wind to cause fear.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6001.meaning: Time can feel like a powerful force that stops us when we face big challenges.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6001.context: Bhima stands at a river crossing where a giant snake waits to stop him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6002.meaning: Danger can appear quickly and without warning, so we must always stay alert.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6002.context: A hungry and fierce snake named Prudaku suddenly moves close to attack the hero.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6003.meaning: Unexpected shocks can confuse our minds and make it hard to think clearly.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6003.context: The snake touches Bhima and his senses become confused by the sudden magical power.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6004.meaning: Even the strongest people can face opponents who are more powerful than they are.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6004.context: Bhima has the strength of ten thousand elephants, but this snake is even stronger.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6005.meaning: Sometimes we feel trapped or stuck, even when we try very hard to move forward.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6005.context: The shining snake subdues Bhima, and the hero cannot move because of the struggle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6006.meaning: Physical strength alone is not enough to win every battle or overcome every enemy.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6006.context: Bhima is as strong as a lion, but the snake captures him with its power.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6007.meaning: We must accept that some situations are beyond our control and require patience.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6007.context: Bhima tries very hard to free himself, but he cannot resist the snake's hold.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6008.meaning: Humility is important because no one is truly invincible against all possible dangers.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6008.context: The mighty Bhima is finally subdued by the snake, showing the snake's great power.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6400.meaning: Time moves in vast cycles that are hard to grasp. We should focus on living well in the present moment rather than worrying about distant future events.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6400.context: The text describes how time is measured in divine cycles using years and fractions. It sets the stage for understanding cosmic ages.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6402.meaning: Even in difficult times, there is a natural order. Understanding this helps us accept change and find peace amidst the chaos of the world.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6402.context: This verse explains the duration of the Kali Yuga and how its time is calculated. It marks the beginning of a dark age.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6403.meaning: All things come to an end eventually. Accepting this truth helps us let go of attachments and prepare for new beginnings with a calm heart.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6403.context: The passage notes that the Kali age is ending and the cycle of ages is complete. It marks a transition point in time.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6404.meaning: The world changes constantly and nothing lasts forever. True wisdom comes from knowing that destruction is just part of the natural cycle of life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6404.context: It describes the end of Brahma's day when the universe is destroyed. Wise people understand this cycle of creation and destruction.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6405.meaning: When honesty disappears, society suffers greatly. We must choose to tell the truth and act with integrity, even when others around us do not.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6405.context: At the end of the age, truth fades away and people become dishonest. Society loses its moral foundation and integrity.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6406.meaning: Generosity and duty are the glue of society. When we stop caring for others and neglect our responsibilities, the community falls apart and loses its spirit.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6406.context: Sacred rituals and acts of charity disappear as the age declines. People stop giving and stop honoring their spiritual duties.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6408.meaning: Discipline and learning keep us grounded. When we ignore wisdom and lose self-control, we drift away from our true purpose and become confused.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6408.context: Scholars stop studying sacred texts and abandon their pure lifestyles. They begin to eat anything and lose their spiritual discipline.
